## Introduction {#sec-intro}

### Purpose

Since defending my prospectus, I've developed, deployed, and refined a raft of models that carry out my express research agenda: revisiting three significant contributions to the literature on international economic policy and human rights using machine-learning and spatial-econometric methods. The object of this first draft is to lucidly describe these models and both illustrate and comment on my central findings. Accordingly, integration of the literature reviews (which appear in my prospectus and elsewhere) await the second draft.

### Contributions

The primary advancements my dissertation endeavors to accomplish are methodological and theoretical. First, in a broad sense, I unite several debiasing techniques, forming a coherent-yet-flexible system for enhanced inferential robustness---one that I expect to be especially-promising to political scientists. More precisely, though each procedure is not novel on its own, their assembly presents a recipe (or workflow) to tackle biases compromising quality inference that observational studies may reasonably encounter, jointly or in part: selection bias due to missing data (multiple imputation), omitted-variable bias due to geographic dependencies (spatial lagging), and both regularization and overfitting bias due to naive use of machine learners (double/debiased machine learning). Each component (or "step" in the recipe/workflow) naturally allows for alternative specifications and design choices, such that researchers may readily implement adaptations suited to their work's *sui generis* dimensions (e.g., data idiosyncrasies, apposite theory, hardware capabilities, etc.). The keystone of this system---double/debiased machine learning, or DML---is a relatively recent innovation, and (perhaps) as such is poorly-attested in the extant political-science literature.[^1] By delineating and deploying it, I thus also contribute to the ongoing introduction of the DML method to the political-science community.

[^1]: Indeed, at the time of writing, a brief search located two articles in the American Political Science Review leveraging DML (Ratkovic, 2023; Jares & Malhotra, 2025), but none in other major journals such as the American Journal of Political Science, International Organization, and International Security, *inter alia*.

Second, in more specific terms, I intervene in the nascent nexus between spatial econometrics and DML---sometimes referred to as Double Spatial Regression (DSR)---by extending spatial lagging and buffering thereto. The original DSR literature, having emerged from the natural sciences (e.g., biostatistics and environmental science), is primarily concerned with continuous point-referenced data and, accordingly, functions modeling smooth spatial processes (e.g., pollutant diffusion).[^2] By contrast, my primary units of interest---countries---are areal (i.e., regional) and discrete, and the processes at issue are political and economic rather than natural. In this setting, smooth functions are hard to justify: implementing them would require not only rendering countries as points---a misrepresentation of their true areal structure---but also assuming that said processes indeed diffuse smoothly geographically.[^3] Therefore, I depart from the extant literature's reliance on smoothing and consider models better-suited to country data, ultimately selecting the spatially-lagged X (SLX) model (see @sec-gen-prep-sptl). Moreover, in my effort to reconcile SLX with DML (see @sec-gen-dml-fits-final-bcr), I avail myself of spatially-buffered resampling, a technique hitherto unused in the DSR literature. Specifically, I propose a minimally-invasive intervention to ordinary cluster-robust DML, an approach I call *buffered cluster-robust DML* (*BCR-DML*). Indeed (and in brief), BCR-DML differs from cluster-robust DML merely by first partitioning the sample into neighbor-wise disjoint subgroups along user-specified dimension(s) (e.g., by country), after which cluster-robust DML may proceed as per usual. Very recently, Balkus et al. (2026) have raised questions about the necessity of such "bespoke" resampling methods, a development possibly upending at least parts of the cluster-robust DML paradigm and which I readily acknowledge (p. 15). Nevertheless, as I later argue and underscore, treating observations "as-IID" poses unique complications for SLX modeling; and in any case, their core conclusions do not cover all facets of DML (e.g., hyperparameter tuning and standard-error estimation), as they themselves concede explicitly. Accordingly, even in the wake of their contribution, I proceed under the belief that BCR-DML remains the safest path for harmonizing SLX and DML, motivating my continued reliance on it throughout.

[^2]: In particular, see Gilbert et al. (2024), Wiecha et al. (2025), and Arifin et al. (2026).

[^3]: For a brief description of areal data and the unsuitability of smooth functions thereto, see Gilbert et al. (2024, pp. 17 & 29-30).

As regards theory, I put my debiased methodological system to work, following additional design recommendations proposed in my prospectus to answer my motivating research questions.[^4] The results that follow, in some instances, confirm those reported in the underlying literature, while in others, they differ, challenging or qualifying the theoretical implications expressed therein. As we shall later see (@sec-gen-dml-plr), restraints ineluctably imposed by the DML paradigm complicate conventional approaches to causal description. I am mindful of this limitation, and I forgo strong pronouncements on causal mechanisms as a result. Nevertheless, practitioners need not be forced to adopt an agnostic posture vis-à-vis theory. To the contrary, they remain at liberty to ensure the inclusion in their models of theoretically-salient predictors;[^5] register which theories are (or are not) compatible with their results; and devise bespoke approaches for testing theory aspects, such as by creating and comparing the findings of model variants. Hence, whilst presenting my results (see @sec-res), I provide commentary on the initial covariates I selected, the theories that ultimately seem most or least plausible, and both the motivations and conclusions of my model permutations. In doing so, I strive to not only model engagement with theory under DML, but also suggest where research beyond DML (e.g., collaboration with qualitative scholars) might advantage the theory-building endeavor.

[^4]: For now, I refer to my prospectus for summaries of the methodological problems I identified in the original literature and plans I made in consequence. References thereto will naturally appear, nonetheless, whilst I elaborate on my treatments and covariates in @sec-res.

[^5]: This task is, in fact, not only advisable, but also virtually essential in order to alleviate omitted-variable bias.

### Research Questions

Before proceeding, it may be useful to recall the contents of my research agenda. To this end, below are concise formulations of the questions animating each chapter (in order):

1.  Do human rights conditions in preferential trade agreements (PTAs), particularly when codified as more legalized (i.e., "harder"), improve human rights respect among signatories?
2.  Do bilateral investment treaties (BITs) improve human rights respect among signatories?
3.  Do economic sanctions sent by Western states improve human rights respect among non-Western targets?

### Preliminary Findings

As we shall see, at present, my baseline models' results suggest the following general answers to my research questions:

1.  Echoing Spilker & Böhmelt (2013), "harder" human rights conditions in PTAs are *not* associated with improved or worsened human-rights respect.
2.  Likewise, but contradicting Bodea & Ye (2020), BITs are *not* associated with improved or worsened human-rights respect.
3.  Somewhat supporting Peez (2025), economic sanctions against non-Western states appear associated with worsened human-rights respect, though this conclusion is safest drawn when clustering assumptions are relaxed.

### Overview of Draft

The remainder of my draft is organized as follows:

1.  A description of my methods for the dissertation writ large (@sec-gen-mtd).
2.  Discussions and illustrations of the work and findings unique to each chapter (@sec-res).
3.  A conclusion, wherein I contemplate remaining questions and future work (@sec-cncl).
4.  Appendices (@sec-appx).

## The General Methodology {#sec-gen-mtd}

### Summary {#sec-gen-sum}

The overarching methodology used in all three chapters involves:

1.  Preprocessing (@sec-gen-prep)
    i.  Data wrangling (@sec-gen-prep-dw)
    ii. Multiple imputation (1): missing-data completion (@sec-gen-prep-mi)
    iii. Spatial lagging (@sec-gen-prep-sptl)
    iv. Start-year specification (@sec-gen-prep-sy)
    v.  Temporal lagging (@sec-gen-prep-tl)
2.  Double/debiased machine learning (@sec-gen-dml)
    i.  Partially-linear regression (@sec-gen-dml-plr)
    ii. Learner selection (@sec-gen-dml-lrn)
    iii. Hyperparameter tuning (@sec-gen-dml-fits-tune)
    iv. Final fits (@sec-gen-dml-fits-final)
    v.  Stacking (@sec-gen-dml-fits-stack)
3.  Multiple imputation (2): pooling (@sec-gen-pool)
4.  Replication (@sec-gen-rep)

In the first phase of preprocessing,[^6] all relevant data are assembled and basic coding decisions executed (1.i.). In the second, the multiple-imputation procedure begins, completing remaining missing data iteratively (1.ii.). Next, spatial lags are generated (1.iii.), and dataset start-years are defined (1.iv.). Finally, temporal lags are implemented (1.v.).

[^6]: "Preprocessing" in data science broadly refers to the preparation of data intended for subsequent modeling.

The DML method then starts, first by selecting the specific DML model---namely, partially-linear regression, or PLR (2.i.)---and machine learner(s) to be used (2.ii.). Fits then commence on the preprocessed data, first for hyperparameter tuning (2.iii.) and afterwards for the final DML fits (2.iv.). Subsequently, all learners' final-fit residuals are combined through stacking (2.v.). Lastly, the stacked results for each iteration of completed data are themselves combined, concluding multiple imputation and yielding final estimates (3.).

Occurring parallel to this methodology is a modified replication of the motivating research described in my prospectus (4.). These results---as well as those found from the foregoing debiasing procedures---will be presented in @sec-res.

![Methodology Flowchart. Note that the final preprocessing steps and DML writ large are nested within the multiple-imputation procedure, which begins with iterative completion of missing data and ends with pooling of results.](/Users/briankey/Documents/Academics/Northwestern/dissertation/visualizations/drafts/method_flow_viz.png){#fig-method-flow width="65%"}

### Preprocessing {#sec-gen-prep}

#### Data Wrangling {#sec-gen-prep-dw}

##### Outcome & Treatments {#sec-gen-prep-dw-main-var}

Before running the replication and novel models, I assemble a dataset, $\mathbf{S} = [\mathbf{Y \; D \; X}] \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times (1 + q + k)}$, through data wrangling.[^7] First, I retrieve $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$---namely, [Human Rights (HR) Scores](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataverse/HumanRightsScores) (Fariss et al., 2020), the common outcome of interest. Next, I construct the treatment variables, $\mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times q}$. This second task is far more involved, one that generally demands significant transformations to the raw data to ultimately render them in country-year (i.e., panel) format. How these treatments are sourced and generated---and how missingness is handled---is discussed further in @sec-res.

[^7]: "Data wrangling" is my preferred designation for basic dataset construction and refinement (e.g., variable aggregation and resolution of coding conflicts).

##### Covariates {#sec-gen-prep-dw-covar}

Afterwards, I consolidate the covariates, $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times k}$, creating additional ones where necessary. $\mathbf{X}$ is nearly identical across the three chapters, featuring the following common regressors:

1.  All 26 Varieties of Democracy [(V-Dem)](https://www.v-dem.net/) high- and mid-level indices.
2.  From the [Polity Project](https://www.systemicpeace.org/polityproject.html), Polity and Regime Durability.[^8]
3.  World Development Indicators (WDIs) from the World Bank pertaining to:[^9]
    i.  Trade.
    ii. Foreign direct investment (FDI).
    iii. Population density.
4.  From Fariss et al. (2022), latent estimates of GDP, GDPpc, and population (logged).
5.  Indicators of currency crises and International Monetary Fund (IMF) program membership, as well as balance of payments (share of GDP).
6.  Correlated random effects (CREs).

[^8]: I source these variables from V-Dem and the [Quality of Governance](https://www.gu.se/en/quality-government/qog-data) (QoG) dataset, respectively.

[^9]: These variables are similarly sourced from the QoG dataset.

Descriptions of these covariates, as well as justifications for and exceptions to their inclusion, are all provided in @sec-res.

##### Case Selection & Coding {#sec-gen-prep-dw-case}

During the assembly of $\mathbf{S}$, I make several decisions on handling observations featuring missingness in numerous or critical areas and irregular coding attributes. Most of these cases involve (1.) small-nation status, (2.) partial international recognition, and (3.) post-Cold War transitions.

In the first instance, I omit from $\mathbf{S}$ all countries failing to appear in V-Dem, coverage in HR Scores notwithstanding. Constituting the lion's share of these cases are microstates, as classified by the [Correlates of War (COW) project](https://correlatesofwar.org/). Though this omission comes at the cost of circumscribing my studies' external validity---namely, to non-microstates---it improves the robustness of my final inferences vis-à-vis future replications. Indeed, V-Dem indices constitute the majority of dimensions in each chapter's $\mathbf{X}$, meaning conclusions drawn from imputed V-Dem data for microstates would be generally and greatly sensitive to the randomness immanent in the imputation process.[^10]

[^10]: More on my missingness handling method---multiple imputation---may be found in @sec-gen-prep-mi.

Moreover, I omit Palestine in view of complications originating from inconsistent coding patterns. Unlike the foregoing microstates, Palestine is covered in V-Dem. However, its reported scores are disaggregated for much of the post-World War II period, with Gaza and the West Bank treated as mutually-exclusive observations, making it unclear as to how to reconcile these data with the single spatial unit that the source of my spatial data, [Natural Earth](https://www.naturalearthdata.com/), supplies for Palestine.[^11] Equally important, Palestine---failing to satisfy Gleditsch & Ward's criteria for inclusion in the international system and hence absent from their [List of Independent States (v7)](http://ksgleditsch.com/statelist.html)[^12]---lacks the prerequisite for coverage in Fariss et al.'s (2022) GDP and GDPpc variables,[^13] estimates essential for computing several treatments pre-imputation.[^14] Owing to these theoretical and logistical roadblocks, I abstain from incorporating Palestine into my models, with the understanding that doing so comes at some inferential cost.

[^11]: A discussion of my spatial models is to be found in @sec-gen-prep-sptl.

[^12]: For a discussion of Palestine's exclusion, see the list's attendant [case description](http://ksgleditsch.com/data/iisyst_casedesc.pdf).

[^13]: Only states with accompanying Gleditsch and Ward IDs (i.e., "state numbers") appear in Fariss et al.'s (2022) data.

[^14]: The computation of these treatments is outlined in @sec-res-ch1-treats and @sec-res-ch2-treats.

Also excluded from my models are a few extinct countries, namely East Germany (formally the German Democratic Republic) and South Yemen (formally the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen). Each was a communist state that existed post-1977,[^15] my oldest start-year, but that unified with its non-communist counterpart (West Germany and North Yemen, respectively) in 1990 amidst the denouement of the Cold War. The two countries enjoy complete data for HR Scores, Fariss et al.'s (2022) estimates, and virtually all V-Dem covariates, *inter alia*---yet they crucially lack polygons from Natural Earth, which does not offer data on historical geographical boundaries on which to base spatial lags. To guarantee consistency of samples and clarify comparability of results in turn, I opt to ignore East Germany and South Yemen throughout, even for my non-spatial models.

[^15]: Start years are discussed in greater detail in @sec-gen-prep-sy.

A further consideration involving post-Cold War geopolitical reconfigurations is the existence of several discrepancies in case identification---namely, differences across datasets in the coding of continuities between predecessor and successor states. These present challenges for variable collation and subsequent inference; indeed, when joining datasets on country identifiers (e.g., COW codes), the discrepancies may yield unmerited duplicates or missingness, raising doubts over inferential validity in later modeling stages if ignored. To harmonize all inputs of $\mathbf{S}$, I allow decisions adopted by HR Scores and/or V-Dem---the sources of my outcome and the preponderance of covariates---to override alternative coding schemes in the following cases:

1.  Czechia: coded as the successor of Czechoslovakia.
2.  Germany: coded as the successor of West Germany.
3.  Serbia: coded as the successor of Yugoslavia.
4.  Yemen: coded as the successor of North Yemen.

These decisions being taken, I arrive at my final set of cases. Ultimately, the maximum number of states featuring in my models is 174. For a full breakdown on these figures, as well as complete itemizations of the excluded and manually-coded cases discussed above, see appendices A (@sec-appx-a), B (@sec-appx-b), and C (@sec-appx-c).

#### Making Multiply-Imputed Data {#sec-gen-prep-mi}

The aim of my next step is to handle remaining missingness in $\mathbf{S}$ and hence sample selection bias.[^16] Uncomplicated methods of doing so (e.g., listwise deletion, mean imputation, etc.) are commensurately easy to implement, though these generally rest on the very strong assumption that the data is "missing completely at random" (MCAR), in which case selection bias is unlikely to be a concern of interest; produce unwarrantedly large or small standard errors; or may prove wasteful.[^17] Endeavoring to avoid these pitfalls, I opt for the more resilient method of multiple imputation. Widely regarded as ["the best general method to deal with incomplete data"](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-historic.html) (Van Buuren, 2018), multiple imputation broadly involves the following three steps:

[^16]: Put simply, this form of bias arises from nonrandom processes causing the likelihood of observations' inclusion in the sample to vary by individual or group. Left unattended, incomplete data can easily compound such bias, since observations exhibiting missingness are excluded from modeling entirely. In the context of international panel data, if some countries or years are systematically more prone to missingness (e.g., due to uncompliant or unreliable reporting in authoritarian states or conflict zones, or during periods wherein such phenomena are more abundant), then the externally validity of any subsequent findings will inevitably be compromised with respect to those countries or years.

[^17]: Indeed, listwise deletion would result in the excision of about a third of all my observations per model, as suggested by the data presented in Appendix D (@fig-appx-d). For more on "ad-hoc" solutions to handling missing data, see [Van Buuren (2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-simplesolutions.html).

1.  Following a user-specified algorithm estimating the missing values, generating $m > 1$ complete datasets.
2.  With each permuted dataset, running user-defined models to estimate some parameter(s) of interest.
3.  Under "Rubin's rules" (see @sec-gen-pool), pooling these estimates to arrive at a single estimate and accompanying variance estimate, performing causal inference accordingly.[^18]

[^18]: For more on the basics of multiple imputation, see [Van Buuren (2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-nutshell.html).

Through this process, multiple imputation provides more realistic standard errors and eschews data wasting. It also need not assume MCAR. Specifically, multiple imputation is equipped to handle data that are both "missing at random" (MAR) and "missing not at random" (MNAR) [(Van Buuren, 2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-idconcepts.html). MAR prevails when MCAR may be assumed conditional on knowing what factor(s) explain the missingness at issue, and thus rests on safer footing than MCAR alone. MNAR, meanwhile, exists when such explanatory factors are unknown.[^19] Carrying out multiple imputation on MNAR data generally requires researchers to assemble more variables explaining the missingness, so as to establish MAR, and/or to conduct an array of sensitivity analyses [(Van Buuren, 2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-sensitivity.html). Lacking obvious evidence of MNAR (particularly after removing the cases described in @sec-gen-prep-dw), and guided by the advice that ["\[t\]he MAR assumption is often a suitable starting point"](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-whenignorable.html) (Van Buuren, 2018), I proceed naively presupposing MAR conditions.

[^19]: For more on MCAR, MAR, and MNAR, see [Van Buuren (2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html).

To make multiply-imputed data, I first select $m = 5$. Von Hippel (2009) and White et al. (2011) jointly suggest the following "rule of thumb" when setting $m$: ["the number of imputations should be similar to the percentage of cases that are incomplete"](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-howmany.html) (Van Buuren, 2018). For each chapter and start year, the proportion of observations featuring a missing value is about 30%, suggesting an $m$ in the vicinity of 30. Undercutting this rule of thumb, however, are a few practical difficulties, as [Van Buuren (2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-howmany.html) observes. First, the recommended value of $m$ is likely to be large for datasets with large numbers of variables, and indeed can only increase as dimensions are added, since observations are likelier to feature at least one missing value the more variables they possess. Second---and relatedly---increasing $m$ correspondingly increases the computational and storage costs of the analysis, as each model must be fit on each $\mathbf{m}_{i}$. [Van Buuren (2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-howmany.html) instead recommends setting $m$ to the average missing data rate (i.e., the proportion of values missing from the dataset), or to 5 when computational and storage capabilities are more limited. In fact, the average missing data rate for each chapter and start year is approximately 2%---even when excluding variables that are complete by design, namely the outcome, treatments, and fixed effects---meaning $m = 5$ is more than sufficient under the circumstances.[^20]

[^20]: For a complete summary of these missing data rates, see @sec-appx-d.

Next, I avail myself of [`mice::futuremice`](https://amices.org/mice/reference/futuremice.html), which permits users to generate each $\mathbf{m}_{i}$ in parallel across individual CPU cores, significantly quickening computation time. In addition to setting $m$,[^21] I further specify the imputation method and predictors. As to the former, I choose random forests, a flexible learner equipped to handle both numeric and categorical data.[^22] As to the latter, for any given chapter, I mark all fully- and greatly-complete variables common to every model as predictors, following the "general rule" of "using every bit of available information \[in order to yield\] multiple imputations that have minimal bias and maximal efficiency" [(Van Buuren, 2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-modelform.html).[^23] Finally, I set a seed to ensure reproducibility. Implementing `futuremice` with these arguments ultimately yields five completed iterations of $\mathbf{S}$: $(\mathbf{m}_{i})_{i=1}^5$. It is from these iterations that I conduct all remaining work, pooling the results obtained from each $\mathbf{m}_{i}$ in the final stage.[^24]

[^21]: Technically, this is done by tolerating the default setting $m = 5$.

[^22]: For a complete enumeration of the imputation methods on offer from `mice`, see [(Van Buuren, 2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-modelform.html). More on the process of and algorithm for tree-based imputation can also be found in [(Van Buuren, 2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-cart.html)

[^23]: I exclude as predictors all variables wherein the missing-data rate meets or exceeds 10% for the oldest start-year, since including them tended to result in failed imputations. Some variables are exclusive to certain observations and attendant models, as we shall later see (e.g., PTA scores for Global South states), and thus would logically never relate to others (e.g., Global North states), hence why I likewise ignore these. Otherwise, I am permissive, since the main issues with specifying a great number of predictors---"multicollinearity and computational problems" [(Van Buuren, 2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-modelform.html)---are effectively neutralized by my use of random forests (a multicollinearity-robust learner, as mentioned in @sec-gen-dml-lrn-dcns) and parallel processing. As a final remark, note that among the variables I mark as predictors is HR Scores, the main outcome, a step explicitly recommended by [Van Buuren (2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-modelform.html).

[^24]: Pooling is limned at length in @sec-gen-pool.

#### Spatial Lagging {#sec-gen-prep-sptl}

In each chapter, I run two sets of models: one predicated on country-year fixed effects, the other on spatial econometrics. My preliminary plans for models drawing from this tradition are discussed in my prospectus, specifically as regards chapters 2 and 3; but at this juncture, it's imperative to elaborate not only on why I've instead implemented spatial models for all three chapters, but also on the specific spatial model I've chosen.

The cardinal aim of spatial-econometric models is to enable scientists to control for spatial dependencies between observations in geographically-structured data, where traits of unit $x$ may correlate with or affect those of neighboring unit $y$ and perhaps vice versa. In such contexts, these dependencies may promote omitted-variable bias (OVB), jeopardizing valid inference.[^25] The data at my disposal---country-year panel data---manifestly feature a geographical dynamic, with some observations being spatially nearer to or farther away from others. In addition, spatial dependencies, irrespective of the mechanism(s) producing them,[^26] have been observed in country-year data in sundry dimensions. These include poverty, inequality, corruption, pollution, levels of democracy and wealth, and policy emulation more generally (Ward & Gleditsch, 2008, pp. 2-11).[^27] The ubiquity of spatial dependencies in country-year data and the hazard they pose to valid inference jointly merit, in my view, the application of spatial models wherever such data is of interest---that is, throughout my dissertation---at least as a supplement to traditional, non-spatial methods.

[^25]: Heuristically, OVB occurs when confounders are left uncontrolled, exacerbating endogeneity (i.e., correlation between treatments and the error term) and hence the prospect of spurious inference. Therefore, spatial dependencies---factors that, by definition, may influence treatment assignment or degree---can contribute to OVB if ignored. For more on the relationship between spatial dependence and OVB, see Gilbert et al. (2024, p. 6) and Rüttenauer (2024, p. 6), for example.

[^26]: These may include spillovers or clustering (whether explained or unexplained) of outcomes, covariates, or unobservables (i.e., the error term). For more on these potential mechanisms, see Cook et al. (2023, p. 62).

[^27]: For additional examples of spatial dependencies in country-year data, see Cook et al. (2023, p. 62) and Wimpy et al. (2021, p. 723).

Ultimately, I select the spatially-lagged X (SLX) model over other candidates. I do so motivated by recent literature on spatial econometrics for the social sciences, including Rüttenauer (2022; 2024) and Wimpy et al. (2021), which foregrounds the advantages SLX enjoys over its counterparts---particularly the spatial autoregressive (SAR) model, overwhelmingly the most common implementation of spatial lags.[^28]

[^28]: For more on the popularity of SAR, see Rüttenauer (2024, p. 7).

The SAR model, which incorporates an endogenous, spatially-lagged form of the outcome ($y$) as a covariate, gives way by design to system-wide "global effects": effects beyond first-order (i.e., nearest) neighbors, where an original unit's $y$ affects not only its first-order neighbor's $y$, but also the neighbor of the first-order neighbor's $y$ (and so on); and feedback effects, where changes in $y$ in both high- and first-order neighbors return to impact the original unit's $y$. The upshot of these global effects is that they complicate inference. On the one hand, they preclude interpretation of coefficients as ordinary marginal/partial effects, or how a one-unit change in $x$ impacts $y$, *ceteris paribus*: both direct ($x_{i} \rightarrow y_{i}$) and indirect ($x_{i} \rightarrow y_{j}$) effects differ in value from the coefficients, a function of the feedback loops embedded in the spatial multiplier matrix, meaning said coefficients cannot be interpreted as simple $x \rightarrow y$ relationships in either sense. On the other, the assumption of global dependence is not invariably appropriate: some spatial processes may not extend to the entire system (e.g., the international level, which regional clustering of democracy, wealth, and other variables generally suggests),[^29] or may take time to become fully realized, despite that SAR diffuses global effects exactly at time $t$.[^30]

[^29]: Indeed, Wimpy et al. find that global dependencies are "relatively rare in political science" (2021, p. 737).

[^30]: For more on the implications of SAR's construction, including mathematical proofs thereof, see Rüttenauer (2022, pp. 731-736; 2024, pp. 11-14), and Wimpy et al. (2021, pp. 723-724).

![Preprocessing Flowchart](/Users/briankey/Documents/Academics/Northwestern/dissertation/visualizations/drafts/preproc_flow_viz.png){#fig-preproc-flow width="80%"}

By contrast, the SLX model is highly flexible and easy to interpret. It begins with the more conservative assumption of local dependence (i.e., relationships between first-order neighbors), though researchers may still account for more global (i.e., higher-order) dependencies should they desire to do so. Also, by eschewing global dependence as a starting point, SLX is better suited for panel data, where spatial spillovers at time $t$ may be confined to first- or low-order neighbors. Global effects being absent by default, SLX models need not entail feedback loops, enabling coefficients to be interpreted as ordinary, OLS-like marginal effects.[^31] Equally beneficial, SLX is fit for a wide range of inferential techniques, including machine-learning methods, since it merely involves introducing the spatial lags as an additional set of covariates. Finally, Rüttenauer (2022) and Wimpy et al. (2021) find that SLX is relatively robust to misspecifications of the spatially-dependent covariates.[^32] In view of these advantages, the authors posit that SLX is an apt starting point for model building, particularly absent strong theory implying that a different spatial model would be more appropriate (e.g., a valid belief in global contagion effects, in which case SAR would indeed be suitable).[^33]

[^31]: This point is stressed by Rüttenauer (2022, p. 735).

[^32]: For more on their findings, see Rüttenauer (2022, p. 749) and Wimpy et al. (2021, p. 737).

[^33]: The advantages of SLX are elegantly summarized in Rüttenauer (2024, p. 23) and Wimpy et al. (2021, p. 725).

SLX is of the basic form:[^34]

[^34]: Formula taken from Wimpy et al. (2021, p. 724).

$$\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{WZ}\boldsymbol{\theta} + \epsilon$$

Above, $\mathbf{Y}$ is the outcome, $\epsilon$ the error term, $\mathbf{X}$ the matrix of independent variables, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ the corresponding coefficients, $\mathbf{W}$ the matrix of first-order neighbor weights, $\mathbf{Z}$ the matrix of covariates (or confounders) expected to have a spatial influence, and $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ the spatial coefficients,[^35] capturing spillover effects from $\mathbf{Z}$ covariates on the outcome.[^36]

[^35]: Wimpy et al. label $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ differently to convey that their contents may vary (2021, p. 724). For example, $\mathbf{X}$ may contain both the treatment(s) and covariates, whereas $\mathbf{Z}$ may contain the latter, exclusively.

[^36]: More on interpreting the SLX formula may be found in Rüttenauer (2024, p. 8).

$\mathbf{W}$, an $N \times N$ row-normalized matrix,[^37] is of especial importance, containing the base information needed to compute the "spatial lags"---versions of each covariate from $\mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times v}$ that take the mean of any given observation's neighbors, and the inclusion of which ultimately makes for an SLX model. Together, $\mathbf{WZ}$ denote the spatial lags. $\mathbf{W}$ is of the form:[^38]

[^37]: That is, a two-dimensional matrix wherein each row sums to 1.

[^38]: This matrix depiction is taken from Rüttenauer (2024, p. 3).

$$\mathbf{W} =
\begin{bmatrix}
w_{1,1} & w_{1,2} & w_{1,3} & \ldots & w_{1, n} \\
w_{2,1} & w_{2,2} & w_{2,3} & \ldots & w_{2, n} \\
w_{3,1} & w_{3,2} & w_{3,3} & \ldots & w_{3, n} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
w_{n,1} & w_{n,2} & w_{n,3} & \ldots & w_{n, n}
\end{bmatrix}$$

Here, each $w_{i,j}$ element of $\mathbf{W}$ gives the proportion of any given unit's neighbors one must consider in computing the spatial lags. As a simple yet relevant example, consider a country-year dataset comprising three countries---$i$, $j$, and $k$---and a single covariate, such that $\mathbf{Z} = z_{v}$. For a select year $t$, let $i$ and $j$ be neighbors, and let $j$ and $k$ be neighbors. The row-normalized neighbor-weight matrix would thus be:

$$\mathbf{W} =
\left[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
  & i & j & k \\ \hline
i & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
j & 0.5 & 0 & 0.5 \\
k & 0 & 1 & 0
\end{array}
\right]$$

Furthermore, let $z_{v} = (i = 2, \; j = 4, \; k = 7.5)$. The spatial lags at $t$ for countries $i$, $j$, and $k$ on covariate $z_{v}$ are thus found by:

$$\mathbf{W}z_{v}^{\; T} =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0 \\
0.5 & 0 & 0.5 \\
0 & 1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
2 \\
4 \\
7.5
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
4 \\
4.75 \\
4
\end{bmatrix}$$

As aforementioned, researchers leveraging SLX may opt to model spillovers beyond first-order relationships. In this scenario, one need only derive higher-order forms of $\mathbf{W}$ (e.g., $\mathbf{W}^{2}$ for second-order neighbors) and compute the additional spatial lags, allowing for the expanded SLX model:

$$\mathbf{Y} = 
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + 
\mathbf{WZ}\boldsymbol{\theta} + 
\mathbf{W}^{2}\mathbf{Z}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{2} + 
... + 
\mathbf{W}^{n}\mathbf{Z}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n} + 
\epsilon$$

Though these higher-order lags are easy to generate, they necessarily entail greater computation and storage costs at the modeling stage. Specifically, introducing more spatial lags increases the number of dimensions for each dataset, hampering fit speed and enlarging file sizes, whilst suggesting the implementation of individual models for each maximum order, $n$. Moreover, as regards my research, scant evidence or theory exists on which to justifiably set $n$ beyond $n = 1$. Finally---and in any case---we may intuitively expect bias to be most threatening at the first order, with spatial dependencies attenuating as $n$ increases. Altogether, these considerations motivate me to restrict my spatial lags to the first order, though doing so does not foreclose the possibility of implementing higher-order lags as robustness checks.

To compute the spatial lags, $\mathbf{WZ}$, I first obtain the spatial data needed to derive the weight matrix, $\mathbf{W}$. This data is sourced from Natural Earth, a public domain map dataset containing polygons for all of the world's countries and land objects, and accessed through [`rnaturalearth::ne_countries`](https://github.com/ropensci/rnaturalearth). From these polygons, and for every year $t$, I use [`sf::st_distance`](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/reference/geos_measures.html) to generate an $N \times N$ matrix, wherein each element gives the minimum great-circle distance separating the borders of any two countries. The resultant matrix is structured such that---for countries $i$ and $j$ separated by a minimum distance $d$:[^39]

[^39]: By default, `st_distance` gives $d$ in meters.

1.  $d_{i,i} = 0$ and $d_{j,j} = 0$,
2.  $d_{i,j} = 0$ and $d_{j,i} = 0$ when $i$ and $j$ share contiguous borders, and
3.  $d_{i,j} > 0$ and $d_{j,i} > 0$ when $i$ and $j$ do not share contiguous borders.

Subsequently, I specify neighbors for the annual country-distance matrices under a binary neighborhood-membership criterion.[^40] Of course, one could define neighbors as a country-pair sharing contiguous borders under a "rook" rule; but doing so is to presume that many countries lacking shared borders (e.g., island states) do not belong to any geographical "neighborhood" and are thus immune to spatial processes. This assumption seems unrealistic, so I adopt the distance-threshold rule of 200 kilometers suggested by Ward & Gleditsch (2007, p. 12) to decide neighborhood membership. Under this criterion, with respect to country $i$, country $j$ qualifies for membership in $i$'s neighborhood if $d_{i,j} \leq 200 \text{km}$. Every neighbor relationship being specified, I derive $\mathbf{W}$ using [`spdep::nb2listw`](https://r-spatial.github.io/spdep/reference/nb2listw.html). With both $\mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$---the common covariates enumerated in @sec-gen-prep-dw, as well as any chapter-specific covariates---I compute the spatial lags, relying on [`spdep::lag.listw`](https://r-spatial.github.io/spdep/reference/lag.listw.html) to do so. Finally, I append the lags to each $\mathbf{m}_{i}$, making five expanded imputed datasets, $(\mathbf{p}_{i})_{i=1}^5$, where $\mathbf{p}_{i} = [\mathbf{Y \; D \; X \; WZ}] \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times (1 + q + k + v)}$.

[^40]: Put differently, under the criterion, country $i$ is classified with respect to country $j$ as either a neighbor (1) or a non-neighbor (0). Ergo, no "partial" neighbor exists.

Importantly, in calculating $\mathbf{WZ}$, `lag.listw` produces `NA` values for lags where at least one neighbor's information is missing. These values can be handled in one of two ways. On the one hand, they can be imputed directly. On the other, they can be prevented entirely, first by imputing missingness in $\mathbf{Z}$---thus forming $(\mathbf{m}_{i})_{i=1}^5$ (i.e., by following the procedure sketched in @sec-gen-prep-mi)---and subsequently by computing $\mathbf{WZ}$ for each $\mathbf{m}_{i}$. The first option---waiting to perform multiple imputation until after forming $\mathbf{WZ}$---generates values without enforcing the spatial constraints imposed by $\mathbf{WZ}$, where each element *must* be an average of the values of country $i$'s neighbors.[^41] Consequently, the imputed figures are much less likely to approximate the mean of country $i$'s non-missing neighbors---a reasonable starting point for estimating the lags---and they may vary significantly by $\mathbf{m}_{i}$. The second option, by contrast, respects $\mathbf{WZ}$'s spatial constraints, computing the lags more-or-less normally---namely, by directly considering known neighbor values, supplementing these inputs with imputations where necessary. As a result, these estimates tend closer to the mean of country $i$'s non-missing neighbors and are therefore more realistic.[^42] To wit, the second method yields more stable, accurate, and theoretically-valid estimates of the lags across each $\mathbf{m}_{i}$. It is clearly preferable, so for each dataset $\mathbf{S}$, I proceed by finding $\mathbf{WZ}$ from imputed datasets $(\mathbf{m}_{i})_{i=1}^5$.

[^41]: In essence, this would entail switching the "Multiple Imputation (1)" and "Lags & Start-Years" steps depicted in @fig-method-flow.

[^42]: For example, for country $i$ with neighbors $j$, $k$, and $l$, and with respect to variable $z$, let $z_{j}$ be missing but $z_{k}$ and $z_{l}$ be non-missing. Using exclusively known data, $\bar{z}_{i} = 0.5(z_{k} + z_{l})$. Should $z_{j}$ be imputed, however, it may enter the mean operation, in which case $\bar{z}_{i} = 0.33(z_{j} + z_{k}  + z_{l})$. The second $\bar{z}_{i}$ is likely to resemble the first, provided that $z_{j}$ is not an outlier, since the underlying equations differ only by the presence of $z_{j}$ (as well as corresponding adjustments to the averaging weight).

#### Start-Year Specification {#sec-gen-prep-sy}

Upon completing the spatial lags, I specify the "start years"---the year at which at each $\mathbf{p}_{i}$ may begin---where necessary. The exact justifications for these start years may be found in @sec-res; but at this juncture, a few clarifying points merit mentioning. First, they serve one of two purposes: to align with those adopted by the authors inspiring my work, or to test alternative theories in which another start year may plausibly yield different results. Second, the maximum number of start years set for any given chapter is two: although data availability generally allowed for a third start year beginning before those used by the authors, introducing it in preliminary model testing revealed prohibitive computational costs.[^43] Third, Chapter 3 specifies 1990---exclusively---as the start year, since setting start years more recent than this entails inferential risks.[^44] Ultimately, in specifying start years, there now exist iterations $\mathbf{t}_{i,j}$ for each $\mathbf{p}_{i}$, where $j$ signifies the index number of the start years, ordered chronologically.[^45] In chapters 1 and 2, two start years are specified, such that $j \in \{1, 2\}$. By contrast, Chapter 3 features a single start year, so $j = 1$.

[^43]: To be precise, running a task with three start years usually led to memory limits being reached, after which the task would fail.

[^44]: Indeed, because the sample in this chapter is already limited to "Global South" countries, and in consideration of subsequent temporal lagging, a later start year would very likely give way to sample sizes so small that they violate Rubin's pooling rules.

[^45]: For example, for Chapter 1, with start years 1977 and 1990, $j \in \{1, 2\}$ corresponds to $\{1977, 1990\}$.

#### Temporal Lagging {#sec-gen-prep-tl}

To evaluate whether the treatment effects of interest are delayed,[^46] I perform my final preprocessing step: temporally lagging all independent variables---the treatments ($\mathbf{D}$), covariates ($\mathbf{X}$), and spatial lags ($\mathbf{WZ}$)---for each $\mathbf{t}_{i,j}$ with respect to the outcome ($\mathbf{Y}$). Namely, I lag the independent variables by $t - l$, where $t$ is a given year for any observation of $\mathbf{Y}$, $l$ the number of years prior to $t$ from which values of the independent variables are taken and aligned with $\mathbf{Y}$ at $t$, and $l \in \{1, ..., 4\}$.[^47] Doing so transforms $\mathbf{t}_{i,j}$ to iterations $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$, the ultimate datasets passed through my models.

[^46]: That is, whether the treatments require certain time spans to elapse before their effects can be realized or detected.

[^47]: The lower bound of the lags ($l = 1$) is the most basic and common temporal lag employed by social scientists. The upper bound ($l = 4$), on the other hand, seeks to test whether the intended outcome of a policy implemented at the onset of a hypothetical political cycle (e.g., U.S. presidential term) may eventually be realized by its very end.

Temporal lagging is a typical feature of inferential models, especially those concerned with international policy questions and country-year panel data. Nevertheless, the technique poses a few complications for my research. First, absent extant data preceding the first chosen start year, $N$---the sample size of $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$---inevitably shrinks as $l \rightarrow \infty$.[^48] This is a structural feature of temporal lagging and is not problematic *per se*. However, it merits mentioning that as sample size decreases, so too does quality of subsequent inference---a problem accentuated for more recent start-years (e.g., 1990). For this reason, I am motivated to cap the maximum number of lags at a modest level, such as $l = 4$.

[^48]: Specifically, under such conditions, when independent variables are temporally lagged with respect to $\mathbf{Y}$, early observations take on missing values and are effectively dropped as a result. For instance, if the independent variables are lagged by $t - 1$ (i.e., one year), their values for start year $t_{sy}$ appear when $\mathbf{Y}$ is at $t_{sy} + 1$. Because there naturally exist no data at $t_{sy} - 1$ (i.e., the year prior to $t_{sy}$) from which to complete the lag, all independent variables corresponding to $\mathbf{Y}$ at $t_{sy}$ become missing. In the country-year case, this means that for every country, when $\mathbf{Y}$ is at $t_{sy}$, all independent variables are missing, and $N$ is simply reduced by the total number of countries (since one observation per country now features missingness).

Second is the infeasibility of implementing finite distributed lag models (FDLs). An option available to political scientists interested in spatio-temporal processes,[^49] FDLs attempt to capture cumulative delayed effects ending at time $t$ but beginning at $t - l$ by including both contemporary independent variables ($\mathbf{X}_{t}$) and lagged versions thereof spanning the sequence of discrete time points (e.g., years) from $t - 1$ through $t - l$ ($\mathbf{X}_{t-1}, ..., \mathbf{X}_{t-l}$). For example, in a simple FDL, where $l = 1$:[^50]

[^49]: A discussion of FDLs and their utility for political-science research may be found in Cook et al. (2023).

[^50]: For equation, see Cook et al. (2023, p. 64).

$$y_{t} = \beta x_{t} + \gamma x_{t-1} + \epsilon_{t}$$

Here, both $x_{t}$ and $x_{t-1}$ feature in the model, and the cumulative effect of $x$ on $y$ beginning at $t-1$ is found simply by summing the estimates of $\beta$ and $\gamma$.

Typical problems attending FDLs arise from the selection of $l$---an arbitrary, user-defined limit---and multicollinearity (especially as $l \rightarrow \infty$), since each $\mathbf{X}$ is usually highly correlated with its temporal neighbor(s) along the lag sequence.[^51] A more unique complication, however, appears in the context of DML. As we shall soon see (@sec-gen-dml-plr), the DML models I deploy partly rely on predicting the treatment itself from the remaining independent variables. FDLs in this paradigm, therefore, inexorably entail utilizing later treatment observations to predict earlier ones. From our previous example, estimating effect $\gamma$ (i.e., the impact of $x_{t-1}$ on $y_{t}$) necessitates computing:

[^51]: For a brief discussion of these issues, see Mignon (2024, p. 271).

$$x_{t-1} = \beta x_{t} + \epsilon_{t}$$

Nonetheless, modeling $x_{t-1}$ as a function of $x_{t}$ violates an obvious and elementary rule of causality: that cause $x$ must temporally precede effect $y$. Because syntheses of FDLs and DML suggest such impossible event sequences---namely, effects occurring before their causes---the two methods are fundamentally incompatible. I proceed, then, by forgoing the use of FDLs, finding treatment effects at each $t-l$ independently (i.e., for each $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$), though doing so admittedly precludes the potential for further investigation into cumulative effects.

### Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DML) {#sec-gen-dml}

#### Summary {#sec-gen-dml-sum}

After preprocessing my data, I turn to the task of carrying out my DML models. The following section aims to delineate the motivations, architecture, and ultimate decisions for these models, discussing:

1.  Causal inference with machine learning and DML in general (@sec-gen-dml-intro)
2.  Partially-linear regression (PLR), basic DML, my initial design choices, and noteworthy implications thereof (@sec-gen-dml-plr)
3.  Learner selection (@sec-gen-dml-lrn): the considerations (@sec-gen-dml-lrn-cnds) informing my final decisions (@sec-gen-dml-lrn-dcns)
4.  Final fits (@sec-gen-dml-fits-final), generally informed by cluster-robust DML (@sec-gen-dml-fits-final-cr), but ultimately undertaken using my novel buffered cluster-robust (BCR) procedure (@sec-gen-dml-fits-final-bcr)
5.  Stacking (@sec-gen-dml-fits-stack)

#### Introduction {#sec-gen-dml-intro}

Machine learning (ML) generally describes the study, design, and application of statistical models that receive and make sense of data to deliver predictions.[^52] Though motivated in the first instance to optimize predictive accuracy, ML methods have become increasingly attractive to researchers performing causal inference, including social scientists. First, they are diverse and flexible, offering a multiplicity of algorithms and settings underpinned by commensurately-variegated assumptions.[^53] For instance, some learners need not presume linearity in the relationship between the predictors and the outcome (e.g., tree-based), or that all predictors contribute to the outcome (e.g., lasso). Accordingly, ML encourages consideration of a richer assortment of possible causal patterns---some, many, or all of which may be discovered to better-comport with reality, thereby promising insurance against model misspecification and consequent bias.[^54] Second, ordinary least squares (OLS)---the traditional workhouse of causal inference---is known to overfit, especially in the high-dimensional case, where the $P$ number of predictors meets or exceeds the $N$ number of observations (i.e., $P \geq N$).[^55] Conventional models are thus vulnerable to poor external validity, a weakness exposed especially in the prevailing era of "big data," wherein a greater availability of predictors can---and perhaps should---be considered to defend against researcher bias.[^56] Finally, ongoing advances in computational power render the most demanding ML methods increasingly accessible to ordinary practitioners. The reasons for ML's allure to contemporary causal researchers are persuasive, in my view, inspiring me to employ machine learners for my own work. Nevertheless, as we shall soon see, simply performing inference with these learners ad hoc---that is, using them "naively"---is a poor substitute. For executing my models, then, I turn to a well-rationalized and comprehensive integration of ML and causal inference known as "double/debiased machine learning" (DML).

[^52]: Parsimonious-yet-apprehensible definitions of ML are surprisingly hard to identify in the literature, though virtually all sources on the topic stress the centrality of prediction and anterior modeling (e.g., [Applied Machine Learning Using `mlr3` in R](https://mlr3book.mlr-org.com/chapters/chapter2/data_and_basic_modeling.html); Baiardi & Naghi, 2024, p. 213; [Tidy Modeling with R](https://www.tmwr.org/software-modeling); etc.). Some, including Chernozhukov et al. (2024, p. 2) and Kuhn & Johnson (2013, p. 1), also conflate ML with artificial intelligence (AI). However, AI is typically understood to encompasses the entire initiative to replicate human cognitive functions---including pattern recognition, decision-making, and prediction---so it is perhaps more appropriate to characterize ML as an AI subfield. The two categories are related as such in [IBM's introduction to ML](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/machine-learning), for example.

[^53]: Examples of machine learners include elastic net (of which ridge and lasso are special cases), random forests, boosted trees, neural nets, SVMs, ensembles, stacks, and more. The [`mlr3` list of learners](https://mlr-org.com/learners.html) usefully illustrates the immense extent of the methods users may consider.

[^54]: Chernozhukov et al. (2024, p. 134) adduce the danger of misspecification (i.e., poor approximation of conditional expectation functions) in the OLS paradigm as a major impetus for the consideration of advanced machine-learning methods and, consequently, the genesis of DML. As we shall soon see, the advantages of such learners over OLS is formally clearest for large, high-dimensional datasets, though their utility extends to smaller datasets as well (since results vary greater by choice of learner in this setting), which Hindman (2015, pp. 53-54) points out.

[^55]: Heuristically, "overfitting" occurs when an overly-complex model (e.g., one featuring an excessive number of predictors) effectively memorizes the idiosyncrasies of a particular finite sample, delivering poor out-of-sample performance as a result. Hindman (2015, p. 49) asserts that overfitting rears its head in political science frequently through "kitchen-sink" regressions, which use not only many predictors, but also many interactions between them. For more on overfitting and the susceptibility of OLS thereto when $P \geq N$, see Chernozhukov et al. (2024, p. 21 & pp. 71-72).

[^56]: Grimmer (2015) typifies calls for political scientists to leverage "big data" for causal inference.

First introduced by Chernozhukov et al. (2018), DML is a growing framework for econometric inference. It involves solving at least two problems---a "main" equation predicting the outcome of interest ($\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$), and an "auxiliary" one predicting the policy variable of interest itself ($\mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$)---in order to obtain an estimate of a true treatment effect ($\hat{\theta}_{0}$ of $\theta_{0}$); hence, it entails "double prediction."[^57] Furthermore, its chief purpose is to mitigate the regularization and overfitting biases that may occur when ML methods are employed naively to estimate $\theta_{0}$, making the approach "debiased."[^58] In doing so, DML guarantees surer footing on which ML-based causal inference may embark.

[^57]: Note that now $\mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$ rather than $\mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times q}$, a notational adjustment I maintain for the remainder of the section. I do so not only align with the DML literature---wherein $\mathbf{D}$ is almost always discussed as a single treatment---but also to emphasize that even in the multi-treatment case, $\mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$ for any computation of $\hat{\theta}_{0}$, since the DML procedure must be implemented on each treatment to find each $\hat{\theta}_{0}$. This point will become clearer towards the end of @sec-gen-dml-plr, wherein I elaborate on DML in the multi-treatment case.

[^58]: For more on the fundaments of DML, see Chernozhukov et al. (2018, pp. C1-C8).

DML is motivated initially by high-dimensional cases, where $\eta_{0}$---the "nuisance parameter" needed to find $\theta_{0}$---is highly complex, usually because the covariate coefficients comprising $\eta_{0}$ are similar to or larger in number than the total observations ($P \geq N$).[^59] Nevertheless, the framework is a general means of achieving valid estimation of $\theta_{0}$, even from datasets where $P < N$. First, these cases may still exhibit high-dimensionality absent a "pre-specified, known parametric model for \[$\eta_{0}$\]" (Ahrens et al., 2025, p. 3). Indeed, the "true" model for $\eta_{0}$ may be nonparametric or depend on covariates unknown *ex ante*---possibilities especially germane to observational studies. Second, in both high- and low-dimension settings, DML guarantees the flexibility accorded by ML more generally, freeing researchers to estimate $\eta_{0}$ (and with it, $\theta_{0}$) using learners of all kinds, including nonparametric/nonlinear ones.[^60] Last, researchers working with $P < N$ data benefit from knowing they may safely increase $P$ if desired (e.g., for robustness checks) without needing to entertain major model alterations, since DML is already constructed to accommodate $P \geq N$. Therefore, even though $P < N$ for every $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$ at present, DML remains a viable and useful framework for estimating my treatment effects of interest.

[^59]: The nuisance parameter ($\eta_{0}$) is denominated as such because although it is necessary for obtaining the target parameter ($\theta_{0}$), it is not of direct interest.

[^60]: For more on this advantage of DML, see Ahrens et al. (2025, p. 4).

#### Partially-Linear Regression (PLR), Basic DML, & Initial Decisions {#sec-gen-dml-plr}

The specific DML model I elect to use is the partially-linear regression (PLR) model: it is the most generally appropriate---additional assumptions must be satisfied to justify the use of other DML models (e.g., those built for instrumental variables or static panels)---and is the simplest, making it the easiest to interpret.[^61] *Prima facie*, the partially-linear panel regression model (PLPR) may seem tempting considering the country-year structure of my data; yet in my estimation, the assumptions on which it rests are too restrictive for my research. Most crucially, it requires no feedback to predictors (e.g., last year's $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ do not affect this year's $\mathbf{X}$) and a static panel (e.g., knowing this year's $\mathbf{X}$, this year's $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are independent of last year's $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{X}$, and $\mathbf{D}$). Although I currently do not model violations thereto directly (e.g., FDLs or LDVs, options discussed in @sec-gen-prep-tl), these assumptions seem broadly inappropriate when extended to international policies and behaviors. Indeed, such phenomena are known to persist, transform, and diffuse over time, and to follow flexible causal processes more generally. Accordingly, it is difficult to accept that the histories of $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{X}$, and $\mathbf{D}$ are even conditionally-orthogonal to the present, rendering PLR a safer starting point.[^62]

[^61]: PLR is indeed the most basic of the DML models: it is built on two equations, clearly capturing DML's double-prediction logic, while also being reducible to an easy-to-explain OLS regression (as we shall soon see). PLR thus serves as the paradigmatic model for all introductions to DML.

[^62]: For more on PLPR and its implementation in `DoubleML`, see Clarke & Polselli (2025) and the [`DoubleML User Guide`](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/examples/py_double_ml_plpr.html). For a full enumeration of the DML models currently available in statistical software, see the [`DoubleML` User Guide](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/guide/models.html).

Having decided on PLR, I shall now delineate how it works in the "basic" (i.e., non-cluster-robust) DML setting. I do so because I occasionally operate within it (see @sec-res-ch1-find), but more importantly because cluster-robust variations of DML are mere extensions of the basic case. Indeed, my cluster-robust models ultimately retain the same underlying PLR estimation procedure, the only deviations occurring during resampling and computation of the standard errors. Understanding how PLR ordinarily operates, therefore, is indispensable to understanding how it functions in my final models.

The PLR model is initially of the form:

$$\begin{align*}
\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{D}\theta_{0} + g_{0}(\mathbf{X}) + \boldsymbol{\zeta}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\zeta}|\mathbf{D},\mathbf{X}] = 0 \\
\mathbf{D} = m_{0}(\mathbf{X}) + \mathbf{V}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{V}|\mathbf{X}] = 0
\end{align*}$$

As before, $\mathbf{Y}$ is the outcome, $\mathbf{D}$ the treatment, $\theta_{0}$ the effect of interest, and $\mathbf{X}$ the covariates. Additionally, $g_{0}$ and $m_{0}$ are the nuisance functions, where $\eta_{0} = (m_{0}, g_{0})$, and $\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ are the stochastic error terms. In the main equation, a user-specified machine learner predicts $\mathbf{Y}$ by estimating $g_{0}$, whereas in the auxiliary equation, another chosen learner predicts $\mathbf{D}$ by estimating $m_{0}$.

As aforementioned, ML estimators are vulnerable to regularization and overfitting biases when used naively. On the one hand, the regularization parameters that ML models ordinarily employ (e.g., $\alpha$ and $\lambda$ in the elastic-net paradigm) may force said models towards simplicity (e.g., shrinking coefficients towards $0$ in lasso and ridge), exacerbating estimation error should they do so erroneously.[^63] On the other, since they are often highly complex and flexible, ML models are prone to virtual memory of training data.[^64] Such learners may then give overfit $\hat{\eta}_{0}$, leading to exceedingly-biased $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ should the data used to find $\hat{\eta}_{0}$ be the same as that used to find $\hat{\theta}_{0}$.[^65] To overcome these forms of bias, DML relies on two techniques: (1.) orthogonalization and (2.) cross-fitting.

[^63]: The example of "shrinkage bias," a type of regularization bias, is given in Chernozhukov et al. (2024, p. 74). Also, the danger regularization bias poses for complex, high-dimensional nuisance parameters---the original motivation for DML---is especially salient, as underscored in Bach et al. (2024a, p. 11).

[^64]: Heuristically, many ML models are deemed "complex" and "flexible" because they offer numerous hyperparameter combinations for users to set. The role of hyperparameters (and tuning thereof) is reviewed in @sec-gen-dml-fits-tune.

[^65]: Put differently, say $\hat{\eta}_{0}$ is found on sample $\mathbf{S}$ using a flexible learner and is ultimately overfit, memorizing the "noise" (or statistical patterns) unique to each observation. Then, $\hat{\eta}_{0}$ is used to find $\hat{\theta}_{0}$, also on $\mathbf{S}$. In this scenario, the estimation error of $\hat{\eta}_{0}$---which includes the idiosyncratic noise learnt finding $\hat{\eta}_{0}$---will be correlated with the score function obtaining $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ (e.g., that of PLR), as the latter relies on the former. Therefore, $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ is susceptible to differing greatly from $\theta_{0}$, particularly when unseen data exists absent from $\mathbf{S}$. For additional heuristic descriptions of the consequences of overfitting for DML, see Ahrens et al. (2025, p. 3) and Chernozhukov et al. (2024, pp. 255-256 & 273).

The first---orthogonalization---serves to counter regularization bias. In the PLR case, this occurs through the "partialling-out" procedure, whereby the residuals of the main and auxiliary equations are extracted, and the former is regressed on the latter using ordinary least squares (OLS), yielding not only the regression coefficient $\hat{\theta}_{0}$, but also (in non-cluster-robust DML) the accompanying standard error and confidence interval.[^66] Specifically, consider the original PLR equation transmuted to residualized form:[^67]

[^66]: PLR is "partially linear," then: OLS is mandatory in the final step, but nonlinear (e.g., tree-based) models are permissible to estimate $\eta_{0}$.

[^67]: The equation here assumes the selection of the standard score function, which does not estimate $g_{0}(\mathbf{X})$ directly, but instead estimates $\ell_{0}(\mathbf{X}) := \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}|\mathbf{X}] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}|\mathbf{X}]\theta_{0} + g_{0}(\mathbf{X})$ (see the [`DoubleML` User Guide](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/guide/models.html)). This explains why $\ell_{0}$ now replaces $g_{0}$. Below, I will elaborate on the role of score functions in DML.

$$\begin{align*}
\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{V}\theta_{0} + \mathbf{\zeta}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{\zeta}|\mathbf{D},\mathbf{X}] = 0 \\
\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{Y} - \ell_{0}(\mathbf{X}), \qquad \ell_{0}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}|\mathbf{X}] \\
\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{D} - m_{0}(\mathbf{X}), \qquad m_{0}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}|\mathbf{X}]
\end{align*}$$

Here, the residuals $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ correspond to $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{D}$, respectively, after partialling out (i.e., subtracting) the effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on each. In practice, DML estimates these residuals using the plug-in estimators of the nuisance functions, $\hat{\ell}_{0}$ of $\ell_{0}$ and $\hat{m}_{0}$ of $m_{0}$, initially found by the learners predicting $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{D}$:

$$\begin{align*}
\mathbf{\hat{Q}} = \mathbf{Y} - \hat{\ell}_{0}(\mathbf{X}) \\
\mathbf{\hat{V}} = \mathbf{D} - \hat{m}_{0}(\mathbf{X})
\end{align*}$$

$\hat{\theta}_{0}$ is then obtained simply by regressing $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}$ on $\mathbf{\hat{V}}$.[^68]

[^68]: This explanation of PLR is adapted mostly from Bach et al. (2024a, pp. 7 & 10-12). For an additional simple discussion of PLR, see Chernozhukov et al. (2024, pp. 249-251).

The partialling-out operation results in a debiased $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ for two reasons. First, the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (FWL) Theorem guarantees that it actually gives $\hat{\theta}_{0}$. Namely, since FWL demonstrate that the population regression coefficient, $\theta_{0}$, may be recovered by regressing the true residualized $\mathbf{Y}$ on the true residualized $\mathbf{D}$---that is, $\mathbf{Q}$ on $\mathbf{V}$---it follows that in the sample analogue,[^69] regressing $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}$ on $\mathbf{\hat{V}}$ returns $\hat{\theta}_{0}$.[^70] Second, in obeying Neyman orthogonality, partialling out alleviates regularization bias affecting $\hat{\theta}_{0}$. All DML models estimate $\theta_{0}$ using score functions $\psi(\mathbf{S};\theta,\eta)$ that solve the sample analogue of the moment condition:[^71]

[^69]: The term "sample analogue" is also referred to in the DML literature as the "empirical analogue." I use the former term, however, to preserve lexical consistency with earlier discussions involving samples $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$.

[^70]: See Chernozhukov et al. (2024, pp. 24-25) for more on the FWL Theorem.

[^71]: This condition may be found in Bach et al. (2024a, p. 12).

$$\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[\psi(\mathbf{S};\theta_{0},\eta_{0})] = 0
\end{align*}$$

Specifically:[^72]

[^72]: The generic DML estimator is expressed as such in Chernozhukov et al. (2018, p. C8).

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I}\psi(\mathbf{S};\hat{\theta}_{0},\hat{\eta}_{0}) = 0
\end{align*}$$

Here, $\mathbf{S} := (\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{D}, \mathbf{X})$.[^73] The function $\psi$ also obeys the Neyman-orthogonality condition:[^74]

[^73]: The DML literature typically uses $\mathbf{W}$ to denote the observations, but I use $\mathbf{S}$ to maintain alignment with the notation seen in @sec-gen-prep-dw.

[^74]: The condition is expressed as such in Chernozhukov et al. (2018, p. C8). In Bach et al. (2024a, p. 12), it is writtenn similarly as: $\partial_{\eta}\mathbb{E}[\psi(\mathbf{S};\theta_{0},\eta_{0})]\bigg|^{}_{\eta = \eta_{0}} = 0$

$$\begin{align*}
\partial_{\eta}\mathbb{E}[\psi(\mathbf{S};\theta_{0},\eta_{0})][\eta - \eta_{0}] = 0
\end{align*}$$

Heuristically, this property guarantees that the moment-condition estimator is insensitive to minor deviations of the plug-in nuisance parameter $\hat{\eta}_{0}$ about its true value $\eta_{0}$.[^75] It follows that DML ensures a $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ robust to regularization bias, a common source of such perturbations in ML. In the case of PLR, partialling out indeed implies a Neyman-orthogonal score function. Under the standard approach:[^76]

[^75]: A more formal definition of the property is that $\partial_{\eta}$, "the Gateaux derivative operator with respect to $\eta$\[,\] vanishes when evaluated at the true parameter values" (Chernozhukov et al., 2018, p. C8). Additional heuristic explanations of Neyman orthogonality may be found in Bach et al. (2024a, p. 12), Chernozhukov et al. (2018, pp. C8-C9), and Chernozhukov et al. (2024, pp. 107-108), for example.

[^76]: The function presented here is "standard" insofar as it is the default for PLR computations in statistical software. For more on this score function's alternative---one that is typically reserved for instrumental-variable models---see the [`DoubleML` User Guide](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/guide/scores.html). For a proof of its Neyman orthogonality, see Chernozhukov et al. (2024, p. 283).

$$\begin{align*}
\psi(\mathbf{S};\theta,\eta) := [\mathbf{Y} - \ell(\mathbf{X}) - \theta(\mathbf{D} - m(\mathbf{X}))][\mathbf{D} - m(\mathbf{X})]\
\end{align*}$$

Accordingly, PLR provides the same assurance as that on offer from DML models generally: debiased estimates of $\theta_{0}$.[^77]

[^77]: That the partialling-out operation (i.e., regressing residuals $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}$ on $\mathbf{\hat{V}}$ to obtain $\hat{\theta}$) implies the foregoing score function may not be immediately apparent to the reader. To obviate any misunderstandings, therefore, I offer a simple proof in @sec-appx-e demonstrating how the OLS solution to $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ may be recovered from it.

The second bias-tackling technique---cross-fitting---handles the problem of overfitting by preventing data leakage, thereby ensuring that the observations used to obtain $\hat{\eta}_{0}$ are independent of those used subsequently to find $\hat{\theta}_{0}$.[^78] In basic DML, the procedure begins by randomly splitting $\mathbf{S}$---an independent-and-identically-distributed (IID) sample---into $K$ folds of observation indices $[N] = \{1,...,N\}$ and of size $n = N/K$, returning index sets $(I_{k})_{k = 1}^{K}$ as well as their complements, $I_{k}^{c} = [N] \backslash I_{k}$.[^79] Next, the learners estimating $\eta_{0}$ (e.g., those finding $\hat{\ell}_{0}$ and $\hat{m}_{0}$, respectively) are fit on training data $I_{k}^{c}$ to return:

[^78]: For more on why cross-fitting helps address overfitting, see Chernozhukov et al. (2024, p. 273).

[^79]: If $\mathbf{S}$ cannot be partitioned evenly into $K$ splits, then $n \approx N/K$. The IID-sample assumption is stated explicitly, for example, in Chernozhukov et al. (2018, p. C22).

$$\begin{align*}
\hat{\eta}_{0,k} = \hat{\eta}_{0,k}(\mathbf{S}_{I_{k}^{c}})
\end{align*}$$

This is performed for each $k \in [K] = \{1,...,K\}$. Finally, $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ is obtained from a user-specified algorithm aggregating evaluations on test data $I_{k}$ that themselves use $\hat{\eta}_{0,k}$. Optionally, the entire operation may be repeated $R$ times, where $r \in [R] = \{1,...,R\}$, in which case the median of parameters $\boldsymbol{\hat{\theta}_{0}}$ is selected as the final causal estimate.[^80]

[^80]: This explanation is adapted from Ahrens et al. (2025, p. 19), Bach et al. (2024a, pp. 16-17) and Chernozhukov et al. (2018, p. C23). A useful visualization of cross-fitting may also be seen in the [DoubleML YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWEoLe8mZqM).

As aforementioned, the user sets the algorithm aggregating the test-data evaluations. The recommended and software-default algorithm (DML2), which I opt to follow, is of the form:[^81]

[^81]: DML2 is the conventional label in both the literature and software. The alternative algorithm, DML1, obtains $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ by averaging $\check{\theta}_{0,k}$, preliminary estimates of $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ solved at each $k$ fold. DML2 is generally preferred over its counterpart because it tends to behave more stably. For more on the two algorithms, including the recommendation of DML2, see Bach et al. (2024a, pp. 16-17) and Chernozhukov et al. (2018, p. C24).

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k = 1}^{K}\sum_{i \in I_{k}}\psi(\mathbf{S};\hat{\theta}_{0},\hat{\eta}_{0,k}) = 0
\end{align*}$$

Here, each $\hat{\eta}_{0,k}$ is plugged into the moment-condition estimator simultaneously, such that $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ may be found from a single equation conducting all $N$ evaluations.[^82] In the PLR case, this entails:

[^82]: Put differently, unlike DML1, preliminary estimates $\check{\theta}_{0,k}$ of $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ need not be found first.

1.  Extracting residuals $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}_{k}$ and $\mathbf{\hat{V}}_{k}$, themselves found by predicting on observations $I_{k}$ with their corresponding $\hat{\eta}_{0,k}$,
2.  Concatenating the residuals such that $\mathbf{\hat{Q}} = (\mathbf{\hat{Q}}_{k = 1}, ..., \mathbf{\hat{Q}}_{K})$ and $\mathbf{\hat{V}} = (\mathbf{\hat{V}}_{k = 1}, ..., \mathbf{\hat{V}}_{K})$,
3.  Regressing $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}$ on $\mathbf{\hat{V}}$ with OLS, thus yielding $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ (as well as, in basic DML, the standard error and confidence interval thereof).[^83]

[^83]: A heuristic description of this procedure is found in Chernozhukov et al. (2024, p. 251).

Further set by the user are the numbers of $K$ sample partitions and $R$ cross-fitting rounds. $K = 5$ is the software-default number of folds, and $K \approx 5$ is usually sufficient for medium-sized datasets.[^84] At first blush, this setting would appear to be a suitable starting point for my work, since each $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$ is approximately medium-sized: $N$ is always more than a few thousand but never on the order of tens or hundreds of thousands. As we shall later see, however (in @sec-gen-dml-fits-final), cluster-robust (and especially BCR) resampling comes at the cost of reduced training-set sizes, a threat to accurate nuisance-function estimation further exacerbated by small $K$.[^85] Nevertheless, simply picking an arbitrarily-high $K$ as a workaround is imprudent, since computational and time costs invariably increase as $K \rightarrow \infty$. In fact, in the context of two-way cluster-robust/BCR sample splitting, these expenses balloon at a rate near $K^{2}$.[^86] With $K = 10$, a modest increase to the default, virtually all of my models feature effective runtimes of several hours (see @sec-appx-g) and the high computational costs these normally imply. Yet they remain feasible to tolerate, particularly with the benefit of high-performance computing clusters, and enable clear improvements to training-set shrinkage.[^87] Thus, in the interest of mitigating not only the burden of model execution and replication, but also the risk of excessively-small training sets for my BCR models, specifically, I hew to $K = 10$ throughout.

[^84]: For more on the appropriateness of different selections of $K$, see Chernozhukov et al. (2024, p. 276).

[^85]: To clarify, generally speaking, nuisance-function estimates made from smaller training sets are more vulnerable to randomness in the resampling procedure generating said sets.

[^86]: This rate increase is not perfectly exponential, since sample splitting under $K^{2}$ cluster-robust DML leaves comparatively-smaller training sets, as aforementioned. A clear illustration of this is provided in @sec-appx-f.

[^87]: For example, for the very first repetition of buffered country splits in Chapter 1 (and using the same seed), the training-set minimum/maximum size is 40/73 for $K = 5$ yet 82/109 for $K = 10$. I am happy to reproduce this result upon request.

My selection of $R$, on the other hand, is made almost exclusively in consideration of cost. Although the software default is $R = 1$, I prefer to set $R > 1$ so as to enhance confidence of the inference about $\hat{\theta}_{0}$.[^88] However, increasing $R$ also increases expenses by $R(K)$ (for regular splitting) or $R(K^{2})$ (for two-way cluster-robust splitting). The smallest $R > 1$ number allowing for the ordinary median of $\boldsymbol{\hat{\theta}_{0}}$ to be drawn is $R = 3$;[^89] yet even at this setting (and with $K = 10$), runtimes are regularly several-hours long (see again @sec-appx-g). Therefore, to access the benefits of repeated cross-fitting whilst limiting costs, I keep $R = 3$ for every chapter.

[^88]: To be precise, as $R \rightarrow \infty$, one can be surer that the inference about the chosen $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ is not an outlier, as per the Central Limit Theorem.

[^89]: That is, being the lowest odd number not $1$, $3$ is also the lowest sequence-length for which a middle value can be simply identified to solve the median (rather than meaning two middle values, as is the case for even-numbered sequences).

A final remark on PLR is that it is, like all other DML models, compatible with the multi-treatment case. Given a $p_{1}$ number of treatments $\mathbf{D}_{1},...,\mathbf{D}_{p_{1}}$ with estimated effects $\hat{\theta}_{0,1},...,\hat{\theta}_{0,p_{1}}$, DML finds each $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ iteratively in typical fashion, the only departure being that for any $\mathbf{D}$, all remaining treatments are added to covariates $\mathbf{X}$. In the PLR case, this amounts to regressing $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}$ on $\mathbf{\hat{V}}$ for every $\mathbf{D}$, where $\mathbf{X}$ contains all treatments not $\mathbf{D}$.[^90]

[^90]: For more on DML and PLR with multiple treatments, see Bach et al. (2024a, pp. 20-21) and the [`DoubleML` User Guide](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/guide/se_confint.html). Support in `DoubleML` for simultaneous inference based on multiplier-bootstrapped test statistics is currently unavailable for clustered data (see the following [`DoubleML` for R GitHub Discussion](https://github.com/DoubleML/doubleml-for-r/discussions/190)), hence why such inference does not appear in my robustness checks.

Though simple, the multi-treatment procedure merits mentioning for a few reasons. First---and most obviously---it is implemented wherever I appraise multiple treatment effects simultaneously. Second, it underscores a key technical constraint DML imposes, one that limits me to obtaining and reporting effects on the treatments exclusively. Because every $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ must be found individually in DML---indeed, the moment-condition estimator permits only one $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ to be obtained at a time---costs in the multi-treatment case rise at a rate of $R(K)p_{1}$ or $R(K^{2})p_{1}$. It follows that if one were to estimate the effects of not only every $\mathbf{D}$, but also all $P$ covariates of $\mathbf{X}$, costs would rise by $R(K)(p_{1} + P)$ or $R(K^{2})(p_{1} + P)$. So it is that expenses would explode estimating every effect of every dimension for datasets where $p_{1} + P$ is large, such as $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$.[^91] The upshot of any such undertaking is that costs may prove not only hard to justify---runtimes may mushroom to the order of days---but also prohibitive, inasmuch as models may reach memory limits, and thus fail, on even the most high-performing personal computers. Thus, for my project, where the great size of $P$ effectively guarantees such obstacles, finding $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ for every dimension is not merely impractical, but virtually impossible. My choice of DML, then, admittedly implies a major tradeoff: quantity of $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ for quality of $\hat{\theta}_{0}$---that is, effect estimates of all independent variables for debiased estimates of the treatment effects.
