This is a compromise with which I am comfortable---the treatment effects are of principal interest to my research agenda, after all---but it goes without saying that the inability to produce estimates of all covariates' effects complicates efforts to elucidate causal pathways, particularly through conventional means (i.e., interpreting the coefficients on each predictor alongside those of the treatments). Theory-building need not be abandoned by accepting this tradeoff, as aforementioned (see @sec-intro); but it will demand more creativity and humility about what can (and cannot) be known on the basis of my statistical findings alone.

[^91]: Specifically, for $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$, $p_{1} + P > 100$ or $p_{1} + P > 200$ is typical. Of course, this explosion of costs is especially encumbering in the high-dimensional case ($P > N$), for which DML is originally designed.

#### Learner Selection {#sec-gen-dml-lrn}

##### Considerations {#sec-gen-dml-lrn-cnds}

A cornerstone of DML, as suggested by its very name, is the use of machine learners estimating $\eta_{0}$. These learners are always chosen by the practitioner, largely after contemplating three considerations: (1.) appropriateness, (2.) cost, and (3.) performance.

Central to any appraisal of the first consideration---appropriateness---is an understanding of one's data. First and foremost, users must know the variable types of the outcomes they specify for the main and auxiliary equations. If the outcome is continuous, they should select a regression learner; but if the outcome is binary, they should opt for a classification learner. Users also benefit from attention to multicollinearity among the predictors, a possibility especially likely in large-$P$ settings. Indeed, some learners are better-equipped to handle highly-correlated predictors than others, such that the former are preferred wherever multicollinearity obtains.

The consideration of cost, on the other hand, is evaluated chiefly with respect to two factors: hardware constraints and user tolerance. As aforementioned, some models may exhaust computer memory, prompting model failure. In many cases, this occurs due to the complexity of the learner itself---particularly at the tuning stage (see @sec-gen-dml-fits-tune), where an appreciable number of complex fits being performed and stored simultaneously can quickly occupy total memory. Therefore, complex learners may prove strictly prohibitive, in which case simpler learners may be not just desirable, but necessary. Further affected by hardware are runtimes, which decrease on higher-performing computers (e.g., those with many cores), but which may still prove long for complex learners. Here, users must weigh the runtimes they are willing to tolerate, whether they be several-hours long or even days long, especially when accounting for any replications they or others may seek to execute. For those enjoying access to them, high-performance computing clusters---such as [Northwestern's Quest](https://rcdsdocs.it.northwestern.edu/start/quest/quest-intro.html)---help mitigate or even obviate many of these concerns. Even under ideal conditions, however, where complex learners can complete their tasks successfully, users may encounter long runtimes when availability of nodes or cores are limited, or when schedulers (e.g., [Slurm](https://rcdsdocs.it.northwestern.edu/systems/quest/user-guide/slurm/slurm.html)) assign their jobs low priority.

Performance---the final consideration---is perhaps the most amenable to rigorous assessment. Many of the most common machine learners (e.g., regularized regressions, tree-based methods, neural networks, etc.) plausibly satisfy the DML-optimal convergence rate requirement of $\hat{\eta}_{0}$ to $\eta_{0}$:[^92]

[^92]: For more on the convergence requirement and the learners that satisfy it, see Ahrens et al. (2025, pp. 17-18), Bach et al. (2024a, pp. 14-15), and Chernozhukov et al. (2018, pp. C25-C26; 2024, pp. 272-273), for example.

$$\begin{align*}
N^{1/4}\parallel \hat{\eta}_{0} - \eta_{0} \parallel_{L^{2}} \; \approx 0
\end{align*}$$

Such learners immediately qualify as possible candidates for practitioners. The guarantee itself, however, only holds asymptotically (i.e., as $N$ increases); it does not imply that learners will give near-identical estimates for finite samples such as $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$.[^93] Hence, in practice, learners may find substantially different $\hat{\eta}_{0}$---and hence $\hat{\theta}_{0}$---for the same inferential task trained on the same data. Additionally, a single learner's estimates may vary greatly when its settings (e.g., hyperparameters) are modified, or when presented with new data. Absent further refinement and analysis, then, whether or which estimates approximate the truth will be uncertain, jeopardizing the reliability of any inference about $\hat{\theta}_{0}$. To wit, "DML estimates are only as credible as the choice of nuisance estimator": if $\hat{\eta}_{0} - \eta_{0}$ might be unacceptably large, then $\hat{\theta}_{0} - \theta_{0}$ might be so, too (Ahrens et al., 2025, p. 34).[^94]

[^93]: For more on the practical limitations of the DML performance guarantee, see Ahrens et al. (2025, p. 26).

[^94]: Bach et al. similarly aver that "\[t\]he performance of the final \[DML\] estimator depends on the predictive performance of the underlying ML method" (2024a, p. 32).

Fortunately, optimizing this choice is easily achieved by following two procedures: (1.) hyperparameter tuning and (2.) candidate comparison. In the first---which I sketch in far greater detail in @sec-gen-dml-fits-tune---hyperparameter combinations from a user-defined sample are cross-validated on the data for each part of the nuisance parameter, and those demonstrating the best predictive performance on the test sets are selected for the final DML fits.[^95] In the second, the tuned models are themselves fit as per DML cross-fitting and then compared by their predictive performance on the test sets. From here, users have two options: to identify the best-performing candidate (e.g., overall or per nuisance part) and make causal claims immediately therefrom, or to first aggregate the residuals from each learner and for each nuisance part following an ensemble algorithm such as stacking (see @sec-gen-dml-fits-stack), forming "super learners" whose predictive performance on the sample will be at least as good as that of the best-performing constituent learner.[^96] Whether for tuning or for candidate comparison, selecting on out-of-sample performance (i.e., the difference between test-set predictions and their actual values) enables users to deliver $\hat{\eta}_{0}$ better approximating $\eta_{0}$. This, in turn, minimizes $\parallel \hat{\eta}_{0} - \eta_{0} \parallel_{L^{2}}$ and the upper bound on the final nuisance estimator's bias, directly strengthening the credibility of inferences about $\hat{\theta}_{0}$.

[^95]: Cross-validation is an operation similar to DML cross-fitting that likewise evaluates fits from training data $I_{k}^{c}$ on test data $I_{k}$. I shall clarify the distinction in depth in @sec-gen-dml-fits-tune.

[^96]: The process and import of learner selection based on out-of-sample predictive performance is described in Ahrens et al. (2025, pp. 30-35), Bach et al. (2024b, pp. 9-11), Chernozhukov et al. (2024, pp. 252-253), and the [DoubleML Choice of Learners Guide](https://docs.doubleml.org/dev/examples/learners/py_learner.html).

Requisite for assessing out-of-sample prediction in either step, importantly, is the selection of performance metric(s). Typical (and usually-sufficient) metrics for regression tasks are mean squared error (MSE) and root mean square error (RMSE).[^97] For classification tasks, on the other hand, users benefit from weighing a wider array of metrics minding not only their research goals (e.g., equally-accurate prediction of both positive and negative cases), but also the composition of their outcome (e.g., balance between positive and negative cases). Ultimately, users have many metrics at their disposal for judging and optimizing model performance. Nevertheless, they should make their decisions thoughtfully, paying especial attention to the metric's appropriateness and likely utility for their desired task.

[^97]: Needless to say, for comparative applications (e.g., determining whether the performance indicator for one learner is larger, smaller, or similar to others'), the two metrics essentially convey the same information, insofar as the latter is simply the square root of the former. They are the default performance metrics for `DoubleML` and `mlr3`, respectively. For the former, see the [DoubleML Choice of Learners Guide](https://docs.doubleml.org/dev/examples/learners/py_learner.html). For the latter, see `?mlr3::default_measures()`.

##### Decisions {#sec-gen-dml-lrn-dcns}

Guided by considerations of appropriateness, cost, and performance, I choose the two primary regularized-regression learners (lasso and ridge) and two of the most commonplace tree-based learners in the DML literature (random forests and boosted trees).[^98] Below, I shall justify these selections. Though I ultimately opt to form a super learner from these "base" learners following the short-stacking algorithm, I shall detail why and how I do so later (@sec-gen-dml-fits-stack), since short-stacking concludes the full DML operation and is thus best understood after becoming acquainted with its anterior procedures.

[^98]: As they are well-established and exceedingly commonplace in econometric, machine-learning, and other research and applied settings, the candidate learners considered herein will not be described in depth. That is, cursory research should normally suffice to locate the *ad rem* algorithms and procedures. As to ridge, lasso, and elastic net, however, the author submits Hastie et al. (2017, pp. 61-73) and the [`glmnet` Vignette](https://glmnet.stanford.edu/articles/glmnet.html) as useful theoretical and practical primers.

###### Regularized-Regression Learners {#sec-gen-dml-lrn-dcns-regz}

**(1.) Appropriateness.** Since my treatments (i.e., auxiliary-equation outcomes) are either continuous or binary,[^99] lasso and ridge---as with most qualifying machine learners---are minimally appropriate, being compatible with both regression and classification tasks.[^100] Additionally---and more vitally---lasso and ridge are suitable for multicollinear environments, such as datasets $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$, which indeed feature highly-correlated predictors (e.g., the V-Dem indicators, covariates $\mathbf{X}$ and spatial lags $\mathbf{WZ}$, etc.). Specifically, these regularized-regression learners are empowered to shrink the coefficients of correlated features. To do so, lasso may perform feature selection, shrinking these coefficients all the way to $0$, whereas ridge may shrink them towards each other, to but never at $0$.[^101] In theory, ridge should outperform lasso when multicollinearity prevails. Indeed, when presented with both highly-correlated predictors and changing model specifications (e.g., new training data during cross-fitting), lasso's choices tend to vary, raising the likelihood of inconsistent estimates. Ridge, meanwhile, permits all features to contribute to their prediction task in some form, in which case their joint influence on the outcome should be more similar fit-to-fit.[^102] Because the true data-generating process (DGP) for my samples is unknown, however, it is also unknown which model will generally perform better *ex ante*. Allowing that lasso may be found to outperform ridge, I proceed agnostically, running my models using each respective learner.

[^99]: Recall that HR Scores, a continuous variable, is the outcome of interest for each chapter. This means that every main equation features a continuous outcome.

[^100]: Lasso and ridge, specifically, may execute either task by setting the algorithm as linear for the former or logistic for the latter.

[^101]: For more on the basic behavior of lasso and ridge given multicollinearity, see the [`glmnet` Vignette](https://glmnet.stanford.edu/articles/glmnet.html).

[^102]: Ridge's general superiority over lasso in the multicollinear setting is especially true when $N > P$ (e.g., for datasets such as $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$). For more on the limitations of lasso and advantages of ridge vis-à-vis multicollinearity, see Hastie et al. (2015, p. 56) and Zou & Hastie (2005, p. 302).

**(2.) Cost.** Regularized-regression learners such as lasso and ridge are relatively inexpensive. First, they enjoy fast runtimes and occupy little memory, since each estimate need only rely on a single solution to a least-squares optimization problem. Second, they are easy to tune. Indeed, the maximum number of hyperparameters that any of these learners may tune is $2$---though only $1$ for lasso and ridge---such that one may reasonably capture the spectra of possible hyperparameter values (and their combinations, where applicable) with lower-resolution tuning grids.[^103] This, in turn, means regularized-regression learners promise quick runtimes and lower-memory usage still further.[^104] By contrast, tree-based learners, which handle multicollinearity at least as well as lasso and ridge (see @sec-gen-dml-lrn-dcns-tree), are far more costly. On the one hand, to produce a single estimate, tree-based learners must aggregate the results of hundreds or thousands of fitted trees, a procedure necessarily entailing larger time and memory expenses. On the other, a higher number of hyperparameters demand (or are available for) specification and ought to be tuned accordingly; for example, following recommendations set forth in Bischl et al. (2023), [`mlr3`](https://mlr3tuningspaces.mlr-org.com/index.html) gives default tuning spaces of $4$ and $8$ hyperparameters, respectively, for random forests and boosted trees. Higher-resolution tuning grids are thus essential, compounding already-great time and memory requirements.[^105] Ultimately, these costs proved prohibitively expensive on my personal computer: model failure due to memory limits being reached was unavoidable, even at the tuning stage. As such, I first run the batch of models deploying regularized-regression learners, since it is the easiest to complete immediately.

[^103]: Specifically, elastic-net models usually tune for both $\alpha$ and $\lambda$, whereas ridge ($\alpha = 0$) and lasso ($\alpha = 1$) models may only tune $\lambda$. Tuning grids are discussed in greater detail in @sec-gen-dml-fits-tune.

[^104]: To be precise, low-resolution tuning grids entail a smaller number of tuning fits and *ipso facto* shorter runtimes.

[^105]: A common solution to the problem of capturing hyperparameter combinations efficiently in a high-dimensional tuning space is to randomly draw such combinations a relatively-low, user-specified number of times (e.g., via [`mlr3tuning::tnr("random_search")`](https://mlr3tuning.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_tuners_random_search.html).) However, allowing combinations to be sampled at irregular intervals likewise allows the grid to ignore significant sections of the full tuning space. This, in turn, heightens the risk that the "best" performing combination from among those sampled---and thus selected for the final DML fits---will actually be poor-performing, a possibility becoming all the more likely as the grid's resolution shrinks. Because high-performing learners are essential to boosting confidence about $\hat{\theta}_{0}$, I avoid randomly-selected hyperparameters, accepting the added expenses my doing so entails.

**(3.) Performance.** The regularized-regression learners, as we have already seen, are equipped to handle multicollinearity, meaning it is reasonable to expect that tuned lasso and ridge models will perform competitively in estimating $\eta_{0}$ (and thus $\theta_{0}$) given datasets $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$. Additionally, we may expect lasso and ridge to perform especially well for nuisance-part functions that are more nearly linear, since both are fundamentally linear algorithms. Finally, between the two, we may anticipate that ridge will perform the best, given its aforementioned stabler tendencies in the multicollinear setting.

###### Tree-Based Learners {#sec-gen-dml-lrn-dcns-tree}

**(1.) Appropriateness.** Random forests and boosted trees are commonly-used tree-based learners, appearing frequently alongside lasso and ridge in the DML literature.[^106] Like the regularized-regression learners, random forests and boosted trees can solve regression or classification tasks and are hence minimally appropriate. More importantly, tree-based learners, which randomly select features to inform their decision rules, virtually guarantee that only subsets of highly-correlated predictors contribute to any given tree; as such, their predictions are robust to multicollinearity.[^107] There exists no reason to expect either random forests or boosted trees to perform better in the multicollinear-setting, so I run my models without prioritizing one over the other.

[^106]: Clear examples of this are Ahrens et al. (2025b) and Bach et al. (2024b).

[^107]: For more on this strength of tree-based learners, see [Kuhn & Johnson (2019)](https://feat.engineering/11-Greedy_Search_Methods.html#sec-recursive-feature-elimination), for instance.

**(2.) Cost.** As aforementioned (see @sec-gen-dml-lrn-dcns-regz), the chief drawback of tree-based models are the large expenses they normally demand. Fortunately, I am able to overcome any prohibitive limitations these costs impose with my access to Northwestern's high-performance computing cluster, Quest. In brief, Quest allows users to parallelize tasks across not only cores, but also the nodes (i.e., individual computers) accommodating them.[^108] Accessing high-performance computing, then, I can raise effective memory limits and lower overall runtimes dramatically, rendering tree-based models feasible to implement.

[^108]: Parallelization is discussed further in the following section (@sec-gen-dml-fits-soha).

**(3.) Performance.** As we have already seen, tree-based learners handle multicollinearity and can thus be expect to perform well on my data. Also, these learners are highly-flexible and thus capable of capturing relationships both simple and complex, including nonlinear ones. Therefore, we may reasonably expect random forests and boosted trees to perform well generally, but especially for nonlinear nuisance-part functions.

#### Fits {#sec-gen-dml-fits}

##### Software & Hardware {#sec-gen-dml-fits-soha}

Having chosen my learners, I proceed with tuning and fitting my DML models. These tasks are accomplished using software I select following careful deliberation and on the hardware at my disposal.

Presently, there exist two comprehensive open-source DML packages: [`EconML`](https://www.pywhy.org/EconML/) and [`DoubleML`](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/index.html). Whereas `EconML` is built for business applications whose main estimands of interest are individual-level causal responses, `DoubleML` is optimized for inference on population-wide treatment effects (e.g., the goal of academic research such as mine).[^109] Also---and perhaps more significantly---whereas `EconML` is exclusive to Python, `DoubleML` is available in both Python and R. In this regard, `DoubleML` is more flexible, allowing users comfortable with each language to pivot between versions if desired or needed (e.g., to take advantage of features offered in one but not both, or to seek improved performance from switching). For these reasons---and since R is my primary statistical programming language---I opt to work with `DoubleML`, deeming it to be the safer, more suitable choice for me personally.

[^109]: See the [`EconML` User Guide](https://www.pywhy.org/EconML/spec/overview.html) for more on its areas of emphasis. `DoubleML` can perform some inference on heterogeneous treatment effects, but only in Python. For more on this, see the [`DoubleML` User Guide](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/guide/heterogeneity.html).

Coding initially with the R version, I intermittently experimented with Python's as well. Eventually, however, I settled on R's for all remaining work by reason of user-friendliness, performance, and speed. First, between [`scikit-learn`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) and [`mlr3`](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com/)---the main dependencies for `DoubleML` in Python and R, respectively---the latter offered the more streamlined experience, its own dependencies automatically handling a variety of necessary and performance-enhancing preprocessing, pre-tuning, and post-fitting tasks.[^110] Second---and likely relatedly---`mlr3` performed far better than `scikit-learn` in preliminary tests, despite my efforts to align their respective workflows.[^111] Finally, the runtimes in Python and R were effectively the same, meaning continued (and time-costly) efforts to improve the performance of the Python models stood to yield no patent benefits.[^112] `DoubleML` in R, then, emerged as the more sensible choice for my work, providing ease of use and performance safety without sacrificing much---if any---speed.

[^110]: For example, the `glmnet` package, which `mlr3` uses to execute regularized regressions, automatically performs covariate and dependent-variable standardization, $\lambda$-sequence generation, and coefficient reverse standardization. For more on these built-in capacities, see the [Introduction to `glmnet`](https://glmnet.stanford.edu/articles/glmnet.html#commonly-used-function-arguments) page.

[^111]: Specifically, during tuning for the main DML equation in Chapter 3 (i.e., with HR Scores as the outcome), I observed a huge disparity between `mlr3`and `scikit-learn` with respect to their best MSEs. This occurred even though I attempted to manually replicate in Python the automated steps performed by `mlr3` and its dependencies. Of course, the writer must acknowledge, here, that the observed poor performance of `scikit-learn` might have resulted from user error, not any deficiencies of the library *per se*. I have not saved the Python results, but I can supply them if requested, since I did retain the original scripts.

[^112]: Again, I did not save the former runtimes directly, but I can reproduce them if necessary with the Python scripts I kept.

Influenced by both software and hardware considerations are additional pivotal decisions---namely, whether and how to implement parallel processing. As we have seen, a major drawback of DML involves the high time costs that it (and machine learning more generally) oftentimes implies. Mitigating this problem to a considerable degree, thankfully, is parallel processing, a procedure we have already encountered in @sec-gen-prep-mi and @sec-gen-dml-lrn-dcns-tree. In brief, parallel processing for a single computational task (e.g., model) divides work across a user-specified number of CPU cores. Similarly, on a high-performance computing cluster such as Quest, entire tasks may themselves be apportioned across core-bearing nodes. In either case, task parts or entire tasks are then run concomitantly, enabling dramatic runtime reductions relative to tasks completed sequentially on a single core or computer. Owing to `mlr3`'s compatibility with software such as the [`future`](https://future.futureverse.org/) package, parallelization for single models is readily achievable in `DoubleML` for R.[^113] Additionally, with Quest, I can assign multiple models to multiple nodes simultaneously, cutting expenses still further. Enjoying access to both of these conveniences, I duly exploit them, not only making computational costs tolerable, but also expanding the pool of candidate learners from which I may realistically select (e.g., to tree-based ones).

[^113]: Parallel processing is also possible in `DoubleML` for Python through the [`Joblib`](https://joblib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) library. For more on parallelization with `mlr3`, see [Applied Machine Learning Using `mlr3` in R](https://mlr3book.mlr-org.com/chapters/chapter10/advanced_technical_aspects_of_mlr3.html#sec-parallelization).

As to hardware, specifically, I run my regularized-regression models initially on my personal computer, a MacBook Pro (2024) running on the Apple M4 Pro chip, 24 GB of memory, and 12 cores (8 performance and 4 efficiency). These specifications are worth mentioning for a few reasons. First, my machine was able to handle my most demanding batches of regularized-regression models within the span of approximately 24 hours. As such, those wishing to replicate the results thereof on more-powerful systems may be able to do so quicker, but those working with less-powerful ones should anticipate even longer runtimes. Second, though relatively powerful as a personal computer, my machine proved unable to complete my models when instructed to utilize more complex learners, such as tree-based ones, as I recount in @sec-gen-dml-lrn-dcns. Therefore, all my tree-based models are run on Quest, which encompasses a massive number of nodes and cores and is thus easily capable of performing my requested work.[^114] Last, it should be noted that I eventually run my regularized-regression models on Quest, too, to take advantage of the runtime reductions furnished by node-level parallelization.

[^114]: More precisely, Quest possesses more than 1200 nodes and more than 80,000 cores. For more, see [Quest's technical specifications](https://www.it.northwestern.edu/departments/it-services-support/research/computing/quest/specs.html).

##### Hyperparameter Tuning {#sec-gen-dml-fits-tune}

In @sec-gen-dml-lrn-cnds, I explain why confidence in $\hat{\theta}_{0}$---DML's estimate of the true treatment effect, $\theta_{0}$---depends greatly on learner performance. To optimize performance and thus inference, many DML experts argue that an operation common to most machine-learning applications should in fact be "required" of practitioners: hyperparameter tuning (Bach et al, 2024b, p. 2).[^115] Heeding their advice, I subject all my models to the procedure. It is the first step they undergo, and it is the most time-intensive due to the relatively large number of fits quality tuning tends to demand.

[^115]: The import of hyperparameter tuning to quality inference is underlined further in other guides to DML, such as Ahrens et al. (2025, pp. 34-35) and Bach et al. (2024a, p. 32).

To review, most machine learners incorporate one or more "hyperparameters," values users must set but cannot estimate directly from the data.[^116] Rather than arbitrarily setting these values and hoping for high-performance to follow, they may instead proceed more methodically, evaluating automatically-drawn candidates of value combinations in a process called "tuning." Typically, users will define a tuning grid comprised of four essential features: (1.) the hyperparameters to tune; (2.) the resolution, or the number of value combinations to evaluate; (3.) the space, or the ranges from which to sample values; and (4.) the search strategy, or the value-sampling method. They will also specify the number of folds (e.g., $K$ or $K^{2}$) to randomly partition their data. Finally, they will perform "cross-validation." Similar to cross-fitting (see @sec-gen-dml-plr), the procedure first fits learners on training data to obtain an estimate of the nuisance parameter, with which the learners are subsequently evaluated on test data.[^117] Aggregated instead of the out-of-sample residuals, however, is out-of-sample performance, following a user-specified algorithm and performance metric. This operation is repeated for every combination in the tuning grid, after which the candidate demonstrating the best observed performance is chosen for final fitting. In DML, hyperparameter tuning is also usually repeated for every main and auxiliary equation, meaning the entire process is carried out at least twice for any given model.

[^116]: Succinct definitions of hyperparameters may also be found in [Applied Machine Learning Using mlr3 in R](https://mlr3book.mlr-org.com/chapters/chapter4/hyperparameter_optimization.html) and [Tidy Modeling with R](https://www.tmwr.org/tuning).

[^117]: In basic DML, this entails deriving $\hat{\eta}_{0,k}$ from $I_{k}^{c}$, subsequently evaluating the former on $I_{k}$.

My own hyperparameter tuning, using the notation of basic DML, may thus be generalized as follows:

1.  For each $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$, randomly split the data into $K$ folds.
2.  For each DML equation estimating a part of nuisance parameter $\eta_{0}$ (e.g., $\ell_{0}$ or $m_{0}$):
    i)  Define a tuning grid with resolution $N$ and a search strategy.
    ii) For each hyperparameter combination $n \in [N]$:
        a.  Fit the candidate on $I_{k}^{c}$ to obtain an estimate of the nuisance part (e.g., $\hat{\ell}_{0,k}$ or $\hat{m}_{0,k}$).
        b.  With the nuisance-part estimate, evaluate the learner on $I_{k}$.
        c.  Record the performance according to a user-specified metric.
        d.  Repeat for $k \in [K]$.
        e.  Aggregate the performance scores according to a user-specified algorithm.
    iii) Compare the aggregated scores, and select the best-performing candidate.

As we shall soon see (@sec-gen-dml-fits-final-bcr), the majority of my models follow not basic but two-way buffered cluster-robust DML. Even so, tuning occurs in virtually the same manner, the only difference being the sample-splitting procedure, which forms $K^{2}$ neighbor- and cluster-wise disjoint folds.[^118]

[^118]: Specifically, in this non-basic setting, $K \rightarrow K^{2}$, $I_{k} \rightarrow I_{k} \times J_{\ell}$, and $I^{c}_{k} \rightarrow ([N] \backslash I^{b}_{k}) \times ([M] \backslash J_{\ell})$.

![DML Tuning Flowchart (Regularized-Regression Learners & Two-Way Cluster-Robust Resampling). Note that each $e_{i}$ represents an evaluation moment, wherein the candidate $\lambda$ fit on $([N] \backslash I_{k}) \times ([M] \backslash J_{\ell})$ is appraised with $I_{k} \times J_{\ell}$; $\tilde{\lambda}$ the aggregated performance score for the candidate (e.g., mean MSE); and $\hat{\lambda}$ the selected candidate.](/Users/briankey/Documents/Academics/Northwestern/dissertation/visualizations/drafts/dml_flow_viz_1.png){#fig-dml-flow_1}

In most instances, I tune hewing to or starting from `DoubleML` and `mlr3`'s default settings and recommendations. The reason I do so is twofold: to promote model simplicity and to safeguard against selecting the worst-performing specifications.[^119] First, as indicated above, I cross-validate using folds split from the full sample (i.e., $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$), which is in keeping with the `DoubleML` default.[^120] Though users may optionally cross-validate on each fold drawn for the final DML fits (see @sec-gen-dml-fits-final), I refrain from doing so because it is $K$- or $K^{2}$-times more costly and known to perform similarly to full-sample cross-validation in any case.[^121]

[^119]: To clarify my logic on the latter point, if default settings are "good enough" for most applications, then they are highly-likely to outperform at least some alternative settings. Hence, the defaults should be regarded as minimally safe, insofar as one can reasonably expect them to not be worst-performing settings.

[^120]: For more on this default---as well as its alternative---see the [`DoubleML` User Guide](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/guide/learners.html) section on hyperparameter tuning.

[^121]: To be precise, the cost of on-fold tuning is $K_{DML}*K_{CV}$ or $K^{2}_{DML}*K^{2}_{CV}$: the number of folds selected for DML cross-fitting times the number of desired cross-validation folds. The similar performance of full-sample and on-fold cross-validated tuning is proven in Bach et al. (2024b, pp. 8-9).

Next, I begin to define the tuning grid, specifying the hyperparameters and spaces thereof. For the regularized-regression models, defined by hyperparameters $\lambda$ and $\alpha$, I exclusively tune $\lambda$, since lasso and ridge require $\alpha = 1$ and $\alpha = 0$, respectively. To do so, I set $\alpha$ properly and specify the space from which the $\lambda$ values will be sampled---namely, the range `mlr3` recommends for models using `glmnet`, the main dependency supporting regularized-regression tasks in the `mlr3` ecosystem.[^122] For the tree-based models, I tune:

[^122]: Note that users wishing to tune `lambda` must do so through the $s$ parameter. For an explanation, see `mlr3`'s documentation on the [`glmnet` regression learner](https://mlr3learners.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_learners_regr.glmnet.html).

- Random forests
  1.  `mtry.ratio`
  2.  `replace`
  3.  `sample.fraction`
- Boosted trees
  1.  `eta`
  2.  `nrounds`
  3.  `max_depth`
  4.  `colsample_bytree`
  5.  `lambda`
  6.  `subsample`
  7.  `min_child_weight`

These mostly correspond to the `mlr3`-recommended tuning hyperparameters for tasks using `ranger` (random forests) and `xgboost` (boosted trees). For random forests, although `num.trees` is among the four hyperparameters recommended to tune, I set it at $500$ throughout to limit runtimes, and because increasing it did not yield noticeable performance gains. Likewise, `alpha` and `colsample_bylevel` are tuning-recommended for boosted trees, though I set them both to $1$ in the interest of simplification and since changes thereto did not meaningfully affect performance. The tuning space of each remaining hyperparameter either follows the `mlr3` recommendation or narrows it based on preliminary testing pointing to better or more-efficient performance along a truncated portion of the original range.[^123]

[^123]: Note that `min_child_weight`, for boosted trees, is not among the Bischl et al. (2023) recommendations, though `mlr3` does provide ranges for it on account of other authors' advice. Ultimately, I tune the hyperparameter because doing so seems to improve performance. For all recommended tuning hyperparameters and spaces, see the [`mlr3tuningspaces` defaults](https://mlr3tuningspaces.mlr-org.com/reference/mlr_tuning_spaces_default.html). For the tuning ranges I ultimately specify for each task, please refer to my code (accessible in my dissertation's [Github repository](https://github.com/bkey15/dissertation)).

Afterwards, I finalize the tuning grid by fixing its search strategy and resolution. For the regularized-regression learners, I employ a "grid" search, which finds $N$ equally-spaced points between and inclusive of the tuning ranges' lower and upper bounds. For the tree-based learners, on the other hand, I specify a "random" search, which draws $N$ combinations of values from the pre-defined tuning spaces stochastically. Informing these choices primarily is the consideration of cost. Specifically, although the nonrandom grid search is the ideal, guaranteeing a consistent and predictably-spaced draw of possible values, capturing a representative sample at a relatively-low resolution with it is only feasible when the total number of hyperparameters to tune is small. Indeed, if one's goal is to evaluate $N$ points along each range, then the grid will grow exponentially for each hyperparameter added thereto.[^124] Since the regularized-regression learners tune a single hyperparameter, $\lambda$, I can comfortably deploy the grid search whenever I use them. By contrast, the tree-based learners tune a greater number of hyperparameters, and their computational expenses are far higher in the first place. To keep costs tolerable for the tree-based models, I resort to random searches, conceding that they may occasionally miss more high-performing combinations. Ultimately, I set resolutions of $N = 10$ and $N = 12$ for the regularized-regression and tree-based grids, respectively, as increases beyond these seemed (in testing) to neither yield meaningful gains to performance nor substantively change my results.

[^124]: To illustrate, take the elastic-net case, which tunes two hyperparameters, $\lambda$ and $\alpha$. Setting $N = 10$ will result in a $10^{2}$-row grid containing all combinations of the sampled $\lambda$ and $\alpha$ values.

Last, as to the performance metrics, I keep the `mlr3` default of MSE for regression tasks, but I depart from said default for classification tasks, opting for log loss in lieu of classification error. I shall elaborate on this latter choice when I cover Chapter 3 (@sec-res-ch3), as it is the only instance wherein I consider classification tasks. Irrespective of task, however, I aggregate the performance scores as per the `mlr3` default algorithm, which simply averages the scores found from each $k \in [K]$ evaluation on test set $I_{k}$ per $n \in [N]$ candidate.[^125] In the case of the regularized regressions, for example, this results in a mean MSE for each $\lambda$, and that with the lowest mean is chosen for the final DML fits (see @fig-dml-flow_1).[^126]

[^125]: See the [Measure Class help file](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com/reference/Measure.html) for more on the default score aggregator.

[^126]: Put differently, with respect to the regularized-regression learners, for each candidate $\lambda$, MSE is computed per $k \in [K]$ evaluation of $I_{k}$. If $K = 10$, there will be ten scores, all of which are averaged to form a mean MSE for the candidate. Each $\lambda$ is then compared by this score, and that with the lowest is selected for the final DML fits.

The final major decision I make regarding tuning is to implement grouped resampling. A chief concern of all machine-learning practitioners is "data leakage," whereby identical information finds its way into both the training and test sets. This leads to overly-optimistic assessments of model performance (i.e., overfitting), resulting in degraded predictions on new, previously-unseen data.[^127] Though splitting the data into test sets $I_{k}$ and training sets $I_{k}^{c}$ generally helps combat leakage, since each $I_{k}$ and $I_{k}^{c}$ pair must be disjoint observation-wise (as we saw in @sec-gen-dml-plr), the problem may still rear its head when the data feature natural groupings with unique statistical patterns (e.g., clustering by country and year). For instance, if all $I_{k}$ and $I_{k}^{c}$ contain observations of both countries $i$ and $j$, then the model---whilst evaluating on $I_{k}$---will re-encounter the country-specific patterns it learned training on $I_{k}^{c}$, due to which it will likely generate relatively-accurate predictions and report high performance. However, because the countries appearing in $I_{k}$ and $I_{k}^{c}$ are always identical, the model never considers how it might perform when asked to predict on data for a different country---say $z$. In all likelihood, then, the model is unduly-sanguine about its external validity; and if selected, it will be prone to poor prediction when presented with $z$'s data.

[^127]: Sasse et al. (2025) offer a helpful primer on data leakage.

To tackle this source of leakage, practitioners frequently implement "grouped" resampling, which simply executes set-sorting by group rather than by observation. In this way, training fits are evaluated on how well they predict for not only new observations, but also new groups, since it enforces group-wise mutual exclusivity for every $I_{k}$ and $I_{k}^{c}$ pair. Continuing with the previous example, countries $i$ and $j$ would be assigned to one test set each (e.g., $i \in I_{1}$ and $j \in I_{2}$), such that $i$ and $j$ would also complement each other in the accompanying training sets (e.g., $j \in I_{1}^{c}$ and $i \in I_{2}^{c}$). A model trained on these splits may exhibit "worse" performance initially, since the training fits are asked to predict for a different country with (presumably) different data patterns; but with respect to generalizability, its performance is more realistic, meaning it is likely to give better predictions for country $z$ (and others) if selected.[^128]

[^128]: A useful summary and visualization of grouped resampling can be found in [Applied Machine Learning Using `mlr3` in R](https://mlr3book.mlr-org.com/chapters/chapter3/evaluation_and_benchmarking.html#grouped-resampling).

Although my research agenda is ultimately more interested in inference than it is in predicting on new or future data, *per se*, I still turn to grouped resampling for a few reasons. First, as explained in @sec-gen-dml-lrn-cnds, the quality of inference about $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ in the DML paradigm is only as good as the learners generating it are out-of-sample robust.[^129] Optimizing external validity, then, is indispensable, hence why adopting grouped resampling---a technique that assists in doing so---is unequivocally sensible. Second, my preprocessing decisions imply the possibility of alternative group specifications, rendering robustness thereto an immediate concern. As we saw in @sec-gen-prep-dw, I determined cases' country codes thoughtfully yet discretionally, ineluctably sidestepping other categorical choices. Fortunately, concerns about robustness to these unselected options may be readily allayed through grouped resampling---which, as aforementioned, strengthens robustness to unseen groupings in general---making the procedure all-the-more appropriate.[^130]

[^129]: As a reminder, for finite samples, optimizing out-of-sample performance enhances the reliability of $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ and inference about it, since doing so shrinks $\parallel \hat{\eta}_{0} - \eta_{0} \parallel_{L^{2}}$ and thus the maximum bias of the learner producing $\hat{\theta}_{0}$.

[^130]: Future years and spatial units (i.e., countries) constitute another source of categorical variance, though they prove less problematic: valid inference may still be achieved for the time periods and political geographies defined for each $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$.

Naturally, the primary groupings inhering in panel data $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$ are spatial (country) and temporal (year). `mlr3`---the dependency on which `DoubleML` relies for tuning---cannot prepare training-test set pairs disjoint along two or more dimensions in the manner that `DoubleML` does for two-way cluster-robust cross-fitting (see @sec-gen-dml-fits-final-cr).[^131] Nonetheless, part of the code I write for my BCR procedure mostly replicates how `DoubleML` resamples in this case,[^132] enabling me to supply `mlr3` with custom splits that respect multiway disjointness. Specifically, then---and having identified country and year as my clusters of interest, as we shall soon see (@sec-gen-dml-fits-final-cr)---for my BCR models and for each $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$, I form four sets of spatially-buffered and cluster-robust splits, passing the first to `mlr3` for tuning and the remaining three to `DoubleML` for each $r \in [R]$ cross-fitting rounds.

[^131]: The one-variable restriction for grouped resampling is clearly stated in the reference document for [`mlr3` task class](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com/reference/Task.html).

[^132]: I qualify that my code "mostly" replicates `DoubleML`'s for resampling in the two-way cluster-robust instance because, in practice, they differ only in the use of spatial buffering (as we shall see in @sec-gen-dml-fits-final-bcr).

##### Final Fits {#sec-gen-dml-fits-final}

###### Cluster-Robust DML {#sec-gen-dml-fits-final-cr}

After optimizing all necessary or recommended hyperparameters, I perform the final fits utilizing cluster-robust DML---an extension of the basic-DML framework outlined in @sec-gen-dml-plr---and spatial buffering. In this section, I shall delineate how the former generally functions, since the buffering operation I propose and implement (see @sec-gen-dml-fits-final-bcr) ultimately constitutes a minor intervention thereto. Also, I will give a sedulous explanation for my decision to treat year as a cluster, the problem of serial correlation notwithstanding.

Developed in Chiang et al. (2021) to counter complications arising from grouped data, cluster-robust DML rests on two pillars: grouped/clustered resampling for cross-fitting and cluster-robust standard errors.[^133] The first---similar to that discussed in @sec-gen-dml-fits-tune---ensures cluster-wise independence for each training- and test-set pair, thereby minimizing data leakage. Importantly, multiple clusters may be rendered disjoint at once, such that in the two-way/$K^{2}$ (e.g., country-year) case, cross-fitting proceeds as follows:[^134]

[^133]: Note that I use "groups" and "clusters" interchangeably, since both refer to categories (e.g., countries and years) structuring the data and thus threatening not only data leakage, but also invalid standard-error estimation.

[^134]: My summary is adapted from Chiang et al. (2021, pp. 1050-1051) and the [`DoubleML` User Guide](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/examples/R_double_ml_multiway_cluster.html).

1.  Assume that the data cluster along two dimensions, characterized by $N$ groups in the first and $M$ groups in the second. Accordingly, all observations are double-indexed, such that $\{\mathbf{S}_{ij} : i \in \{1, ..., N\}, j \in \{1, ..., M\}\}$.
2.  Randomly partition $[N] := \{1, ..., N\}$ and $[M] := \{1, ..., M\}$ into $K$ user-specified subsets $\{I_{1}, ..., I_{K}\}$ and $\{J_{1}, ..., J_{K}\}$.
3.  Take the Cartesian product of these, giving $[K]^{2} := \{I_{1}, ..., I_{K}\} \times \{J_{1}, ..., J_{K}\}$ subsets.
4.  For each $(k, \ell) \in [K]^{2}$, estimate $\eta_{0}$ using all $(i, j)$ observations in $([N] \backslash I_{k}) \times ([M] \backslash J_{\ell})$. That is:

$$\hat{\eta}_{0, k\ell} = \hat{\eta}_{0}\left((\mathbf{S}_{ij})_{(i,j) \in ([N] \backslash I_{k}) \times ([M] \backslash J_{\ell})}\right)$$

5.  Solve for causal estimate $\hat{\theta}_{0}$. Following the software-default algorithm given in @sec-gen-dml-plr (i.e., DML2):[^135]

[^135]: Here, $|I_{k}|$ and $|J_{\ell}|$ signify the cardinality of sets $I_{k}$ and $J_{\ell}$---that is, the number of groups belonging to each respective subset.

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{K^{2}} \sum_{k = 1}^{K} \sum_{\ell = 1}^{K} \frac{1}{|I_{k}||J_{\ell}|} \sum_{(i, j) \in I_{k} \times J_{\ell}} \psi(\mathbf{S}_{ij}; \hat{\theta}_{0}, \hat{\eta}_{0,kl}) = 0
\end{align*}$$

In this way, cross-fitting closely resembles the process detailed in @sec-gen-dml-plr, the key difference being the resampling procedure. Partitioning the data strictly group-wise, cluster-robust resampling offers a patent benefit: guaranteeing mutual exclusivity between training and test sets along all specified dimensions concomitantly. Nevertheless, handling cluster-induced data leakage as such does come at a few costs worth acknowledging. First---and perhaps not as obvious at first glance---multiway disjointness can only be achieved by forming test sets smaller than those that would be assembled using basic DML (i.e., taking the simple complement of each fold), a point I illustrate with a simple example in @sec-appx-f. Hence, to augment training-set sizes and thereby improve the quality of nuisance-function estimation, users may need to select a relatively-high value for $K$. Second, multiway resampling entails exponential increases to the total number of folds relative to $K$ (e.g., in the two-way case, $K$ increases to $K^{2}$). In the multiway setting, then, wherein a high starting point for $K$ is normally ideal and $K$ grows exponentially, cluster-robust DML can be a computationally-costly endeavor. However, as aforementioned in @sec-gen-dml-plr, I have considered these implications and found both expenses and training-set loss to be tolerable at $K = 10$, particularly in virtue of my Quest access and even in the BCR case, which shrinks training sets still further (see @sec-gen-dml-fits-final-bcr).

![DML Flowchart. Cross-fitting proceeds as follows: (1.) The first round ($r_{1}$) is initialized. (2.) The dataset is split into $K^{2}$ folds as per two-way cluster-robust DML. (3.) Evaluation moments ($e_{i}$) occur for each nuisance part $\ell$ and $m$, namely whereby the model is trained on the folds disjoint from $k$ and subsequently tested on $k$. Residuals from these evaluations are recorded and concatenated. (4.) Residualized $Y$ (found estimating $\ell$) is regressed on residualized $D$ (found estimating $m$), yielding provisional causal estimate $\tilde{\theta}_{1}$. (5.) Steps 2-4 are repeated $R$ times. (6.) The median $\tilde{\theta}_{i}$ is selected as the final estimate, $\hat{\theta}_{i,j,l}$. Note that short-stacking, as described in @sec-gen-dml-fits-stack, occurs between steps (3.) and (4.), transforming the concatenated residuals prior to finding each $\tilde{\theta}_{i}$.](/Users/briankey/Documents/Academics/Northwestern/dissertation/visualizations/drafts/dml_flow_viz_2.png){#fig-dml-flow}

The second cornerstone---cluster-robust standard errors---adapts a practice commonplace in models relying on grouped data. Within-cluster correlation of errors jeopardizes valid inference by underestimating true standard errors, resulting in erroneous rejections of null hypotheses (i.e., Type 1 errors).[^136] To mitigate the threat posed by this type of correlation, researchers typically opt for standard-error estimators whose formulae are designed to control for it (and are therefore "cluster-robust"). For cluster-robust DML, Chiang et al. (2021) propose estimating variance by:

[^136]: Examples of within-cluster error correlation, and the consequences thereof, are summarized well in Cameron et al. (2011, pp. 238-239) and Cameron & Miller (2015, p. 318).

$$\begin{align*}
\hat{\sigma}^{2}
= 
\hat{J}^{-1}
\hat{\Gamma}
\hat{J}^{-1}
\end{align*}$$

In the $K^{2}$ case, $\hat{\Gamma}$ and $\hat{J}$ are themselves found by:[^137]

[^137]: Note that the below formulae use the notation $n \wedge m  := \text{min}\{n,m\}$.

$$\begin{align}
\hat{\Gamma}
=
\frac{1}{K^{2}}
\sum_{(k,l)\in[K]^{2}}
\Bigg[
\frac{|I_k|\wedge|J_\ell|}
{|I_k||J_\ell|}
\Bigg(
&
\sum_{i\in I_k}
\sum_{j\in J_\ell}
\sum_{j'\in J_\ell}
\psi(\mathbf S_{ij};\hat\theta,\hat\eta_{kl})
\psi(\mathbf S_{ij'};\hat\theta_{0},\hat\eta_{kl})
\\
&+
\sum_{i\in I_k}
\sum_{i'\in I_k}
\sum_{j\in J_\ell}
\psi(\mathbf S_{ij};\hat\theta,\hat\eta_{kl})
\psi(\mathbf S_{i'j};\hat\theta_{0},\hat\eta_{kl})
\Bigg)
\Bigg]
\end{align}$$

$$\begin{align*}
\hat{J}
= 
\frac{1}{K^{2}}
\sum_{(k,l)\in[K]^{2}}
\frac{1}{|I_{k}||J_{\ell}|}
\sum_{i \in I_{k}}
\sum_{j \in J_{\ell}}
\psi_{a}(\mathbf S_{ij};\hat\theta,\hat\eta_{kl})
\end{align*}$$

Letting $\underline{C} := N \wedge M$, the cluster-robust standard error may then be estimated simply by:

$$\begin{align*}
SE = \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^{2}/\underline{C}}
\end{align*}$$

With $SE$, a $(1 - \alpha)$ confidence interval may also be reported by:

$$\begin{align*}
\left[
\hat{\theta}
\pm
\Phi^{-1}
(1 - \alpha/2)
\sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^{2}/\underline{C}}
\right]
\end{align*}$$

As emphasized in @sec-gen-dml-fits-tune, my data manifestly exhibit grouping (i.e., by geography and time), the deleterious impact thereof on inference is imperative to alleviate. Moreover, Cameron et al. (2011, p. 238) emphasize that---for panel data---clustered errors may persist notwithstanding controls for unit and temporal effects, rendering such solutions insufficient. Therefore, in my estimation, it is both reasonable and necessary for me to consider cluster-robust DML.

Controlling for clustering by country is perhaps the simplest to defend: absent evidence to the contrary, I presuppose that my panel data are typical in exhibiting within-country correlation of errors, an archetypal example of clustering,[^138] such that it is logical to formally identify country as a cluster influencing the DML implementation. The matter of clustering in the temporal dimension, on the other hand, merits greater deliberation in view of the unique complications time poses. Specifically, panel data are also known to exhibit serial correlation: observations at time $t \in [T] = \{1, ..., T\}$ may be dependent on those at nearby time points (e.g., $t-1$ or $t+1$), generally due to the behavior of historical trends, which may persist, transform gradually, or change course abruptly following a unit-specific or systemic "shock." Hence, partitioning the data simply by $t$---to wit, treating time as a cluster akin to unit---cannot overcome serial correlation: for example, if unit-year observations $i_{t}$ and $i_{t-1}$ are assigned to the test and training sets, respectively, then these sets are not perfectly disjoint if $i_{t}$ and $i_{t-1}$ are indeed serially correlated.

[^138]: Cameron et al. (2011, pp. 239 & 246-247), for instance, cite clustering by country as a motivating case for their multiway procedure.

Unfortunately, a standard, "best-practice" solution for serial correlation in DML applications has yet to be developed, as Fuhr & Papies (2024) underline most comprehensively. In the static-panel case, Clarke & Polselli (2025) recommend resampling by unit and thus each unit's time series; however, residual temporal dependence may remain, since observations at and near $t$ are eligible for assignment to both the training and test sets simultaneously (Fuhr & Papies, 2024, p. 11). Furthermore, practitioners may resample by time directly using one of three strategies. The first is the aforementioned $t$-wise split rule, which randomly partitions the data by period into $K$ folds. Put differently, time is treated as a cluster and resampled accordingly, effectively ignoring the problem of serial correlation. The second, by contrast, is nonrandom, ordering the time dimension chronologically and dividing it into $K$ adjacent folds.[^139] The third employs a "neighbors-left-out" (NLO) procedure proffered by Semenova et al. (2023), which forms $K$ adjacent folds similarly, but subsequently drops immediately-adjacent periods from the corresponding training sets.[^140] Although the second and third options clearly do more to limit the number and proximity of adjacency points, thereby promising to reduce serial correlation the most (Fuhr & Papies, 2024, p. 15), it is not immediately clear how these resampling methods ought to be reconciled with cluster-robust DML in the event doing so is desired. Namely, if the splitting procedures thereof presume the existence of multi-period "eras" characterized by within-era dependence yet between-era independence, as appears to be the case, then is it more theoretically justified to interpret era or period as the temporal cluster of interest? The answer to this question is undoubtedly of some moment: favoring the former will generally lower $\underline{C}$ and thereby inflate the $SE$ estimate, perhaps incorrectly so, since the number of $K$ folds will typically be lower than those of both the $T$ periods and the units (e.g., $C$ countries).

[^139]: For example, let $T = 4$ and $K = 2$. Then, $K_{1} = \{t_{1}, t_{2}\}$ and $K^{c}_{1} = \{t_{3}, t_{4}\}$. Also, $K_{2} = \{t_{3}, t_{4}\}$ and $K^{c}_{2} = \{t_{1}, t_{2}\}$.

[^140]: For example, let $T = 4$ and $K = 2$. Then, $K_{1} = \{t_{1}, t_{2}\}$ and $K^{c}_{1} = \{t_{4}\}$. Also, $K_{2} = \{t_{3}, t_{4}\}$ and $K^{c}_{2} = \{t_{1}\}$ In effect, then, neighbors-left-out resampling is a temporal analogue of the BCR procedure I shall soon introduce.

Ultimately, I elect to treat time as an ordinary cluster, adopting the $t$-wise split rule and effectively proceeding with two-way ($K^{2}$) cluster-robust DML. Years---my periods of interest---may be serially correlated, but so too do they cover historical "shocks", whose effects may be felt acutely yet briefly (e.g., over a single year or short span of years). A central motivation for the original multiway clustering literature, in fact, was the observed "factor structure" imposed on years in panel data by such shocks (Cameron et al., 2011, pp. 238-239).[^141] Treating country and year as similarly-structured clusters, then, is not only theoretically defensible, but also with clear precedent. Moreover, as aforementioned, simple-chronological and NLO splitting procedures may imply that the temporal cluster of interest is not year but era. If so, they require the user to adopt a fundamentally-different assumption about the cluster's structure---a pivot that may be not only unintended, but also arbitrary. Indeed, the validity of dividing time into $K$ disjoint and equally-long eras, beginning and concluding at the sample's start and end years, may be unknown, such that any selection of $K$ may be hard to defend theoretically. Obviating the need to confront this complication, on the other hand, is the choice to simply cluster by year.

[^141]: To clarify, shocks may prompt years to take on a factor structure by introducing a shared, unobserved component to units' error terms at year $t$, with similar or different effects across units.

To be sure, I do not claim that my recognition of annual clustering resolves the problem of serial correlation. On the contrary, I tolerate it: adjacent years are allowed to compose either side of any training-test set pair. Nevertheless, I already attend to shocks due to their potential influence on the treatment effect as "triggers" (or confounders), as we shall later see (in @sec-res-gen-rem-covar), and I anticipate that care for their impact on the error term will be equally warranted given their possible role in inducing within-period correlation of errors. Therefore, it is fair to characterize shocks as a principal, overarching concerns for my modeling. Faced with a tradeoff between handling serial correlation and doing so for shock-induced temporal clustering, I ultimately favor the latter: on balance---and in my setting---shocks appear more theoretically salient, and as aforementioned, imply the more defensible period-wise (vis-à-vis era-wise) temporal dependence structure. Initial encouragement for my decision to cluster by year may be found in Fuhr & Papies (2024), whose cross-fitting simulation finds that resampling by period yields estimation errors "hardly distinguishable" from those of simple-chronological and NLO partitioning (pp. 20-21), signalling that period clustering is minimally safe.[^142]

[^142]: The specific DGP used in this simulation is their most "complex" (Fuhr & Papies, 2024, p. 19), for it assumes a high-degree of serial correlation and that time-invariant (i.e., unit-specific) unobserved heterogeneity influences the treatment, outcome, and confounders each. For more, see Fuhr & Papies (2024, p. 13 & pp. 19-21).

###### Buffered Cluster-Robust (BCR) DML {#sec-gen-dml-fits-final-bcr}

Having settled my approach towards the temporal dimension, I turn my attention to space. As a review, the spatial dimension---like that of time---may encompass observations correlated through proximity. To control for such dependencies, I have elected to implement the SLX model, which---generally speaking---averages the variables of any given unit's neighbors, following a membership rule supplied by the user, and including these "lags" as covariates (see @sec-gen-prep-sptl). Moreover, I have specified country, representing the spatial units of interest, as one of two clusters upon which my datasets $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$ will be partitioned. Nonetheless, resampling by unit alone will not ensure disjoint training-test set pairs when spatial lags are present: lags in one set may be formed from observations assigned to the other. To illustrate with a simple yet particularly-severe example, consider countries $i$ and $j$, who are each other's only neighbors. Then, when either $i$ or $j$ is assigned to the test set, $i$ or $j$'s data will be almost entirely replicated in the training set as its neighbor's spatial lags.

To prevent lag-induced data leakage, promoting compatibility between SLX and cluster-robust DML, I propose introducing spatial buffering to the resampling step, forming a general procedure I denominate *buffered cluster-robust DML (BCR-DML)*. In simple terms, spatially-buffered resampling randomly partitions units into $K$ test folds, as is typical, but then constructs the training folds by assembling all complimentary units not falling under the user's spatial exclusion rule (e.g., contiguity or distance). Essentially, then, training-test set pairs are marked by "buffers" separating proximate units. Defined exclusively by its adoption of this resampling scheme, BCR-DML constitutes a minimally-invasive intervention to ordinary cluster-robust DML; indeed, spatial buffering simply optimizes disjoint resampling in the SLX setting, such that no fundamental adjustments to the underlying assumptions or mathematical operations of the regular procedure need occur.

![An illustration of spatially-buffered resampling, taken from the very first country-splits drawn in Chapter 1. Note that the polygons appearing on the map are only those countries comprising the Chapter 1 data.](/Users/briankey/Documents/Academics/Northwestern/dissertation/visualizations/drafts/bcr_anim.gif){#fig-bcr-anim}

Formally, BCR-DML proposes a variation on the first few steps of the cluster-robust DML procedure enumerated in @sec-gen-dml-fits-final-cr. Namely, in the two-way cluster case, featuring one spatial cluster:

1.  Assume that the data cluster along two dimensions, one of which is spatial, such that there are $N$ spatial groups and $M$ other groups. In this setting, all observations are double-indexed, such that $\{\mathbf{S}_{ij} : i \in \{1, ..., N\}, j \in \{1, ..., M\}\}$.
2.  Randomly partition $[N] := \{1, ..., N\}$ and $[M] := \{1, ..., M\}$ into $K$ user-specified subsets $\{I_{1}, ..., I_{K}\}$ and $\{J_{1}, ..., J_{K}\}$.
3.  Take the Cartesian product of these, giving $[K]^{2} := \{I_{1}, ..., I_{K}\} \times \{J_{1}, ..., J_{K}\}$ subsets.
4.  Let $b$ be a user-specified spatial exclusion rule. For each $i \in I_{k}$, apply $b$ thereto, identifying any $i' \in [N]$ observation satisfying it. In effect, we now have buffer-aware subsets $\{I^{b}_{1}, ..., I^{b}_{K}\}$, wherein each $I^{b}_{k}$ includes not only all $i \in I_{k}$, but also all $i' \in [N]$ satisfying $b$.[^143]
5.  For each $(k, \ell) \in [K]^{2}$, estimate $\eta_{0}$ using all $(i, j)$ observations in $([N] \backslash I^{b}_{k}) \times ([M] \backslash J_{\ell})$. That is:

[^143]: The resampling software may or may not literally form $\{I^{b}_{1}, ..., I^{b}_{K}\}$ (e.g., for any $I_{k}$, it could instead drop from the compliment $I^{c}_{k}$ any $i' \in [N]$ satisfying $b$ with respect to $i \in I_{k}$). To minimize the formulaic differences between BCR-DML and cluster-robust DML, however, I prefer the $I^{b}_{k}$ notation. My diction in this step thus intends to clarify what $([N] \backslash I^{b}_{k})$ represents: the buffered compliment of $I_{k}$.

$$\hat{\eta}_{0, k\ell} = \hat{\eta}_{0}\left((\mathbf{S}_{ij})_{(i,j) \in ([N] \backslash I^{b}_{k}) \times ([M] \backslash J_{\ell})}\right)$$

Subsequently, cluster-robust DML proceeds as per usual, leveraging $\hat{\eta}_{0, k\ell}$ to find $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ and estimate $SE$.

To ensure that the training-test set pairs are neighbor-wise disjoint---and hence that the lags appearing in one side of any pair are independent of all observations assigned to the other---I set $b$ to $d_{i,j} \leq 200 \text{km}$, the same neighborhood-membership rule defining the spatial lags (see @sec-gen-prep-sptl). Also, to carry out the spatial-buffering operation, I give the Natural Earth country polygons to the [`spatialsample`](https://spatialsample.tidymodels.org/index.html) package, utilizing the [`spatial_block_cv()`](https://spatialsample.tidymodels.org/articles/buffering.html) function specifically.[^144] Though the `mlr3` ecosystem also offers resampling with spatial buffering via the [`mlr3spatiotempcv`](https://mlr3spatiotempcv.mlr-org.com/) package, I ultimately prefer `spatialsample` due to its express guarantee of buffering by edge-to-edge (rather than centroid-to-centroid) distance in the polygon case, thereby replicating the procedure used to identify neighbors for the spatial lags.[^145] Having formed the spatial partitions, I then split time, implementing ordinary (i.e., non-buffered) resampling with [`rsample::vfold_cv()`](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/reference/vfold_cv.html). Afterwards, I take the Cartesian product of the training and test splits, following cluster-robust DML, to arrive at my final training-test set pairs. For each $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$, as aforementioned (see @sec-gen-dml-fits-tune), I complete this entire operation four times: once for each hyperparameter tuning and three times for each $r \in [R]$ cross-fitting round.

[^144]: This function sets $b$ by the `buffer` argument. For more, see the `?spatialsample::spatial_block_cv()` help file.

[^145]: That is, the neighborhood-membership rule for computing the spatial lags is likewise applied using edge-to-edge (i.e., border-to-border) distance. For more on the edge-to-edge distance guarantee, see the [`spatialsample` article on buffering](https://spatialsample.tidymodels.org/articles/buffering.html).

The BCR-DML procedure I put forward entails two primary drawbacks---one practical, the other theoretical. First, as aforementioned (and as illustrated plainly by @fig-bcr-anim), spatial buffering excludes from the training set any unit satisfying the exclusion rule ($b$) with respect to the test set. In effect, then, buffering shrinks the pool of units eligible for training-set assignment, forming training sets even smaller than those that would materialize under ordinary cluster-robust DML. Accordingly, BCR-DML only reinforces the need for a relatively-high starting $K$. However, I have identified $K = 10$ as not only low enough to ensure reasonable computational costs (particularly in view of my Quest access), but also high enough to yield large training sets relative to the test sets, buffering notwithstanding. Therefore, in my case, BCR-DML poses few practical hurdles, enabling me to adopt the method comfortably.

Second---and perhaps more seriously---recent literature has pushed back on some of the fundamental assumptions undergirding the cluster-robust DML paradigm. Specifically, for correlated observations---including clustered, spatial, and time-series data---Balkus et al. (2026) posit that valid estimation of $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ may be achieved via basic-DML cross-fitting, whereby sample $\mathbf{S}$ is treated "as-IID" for training-test set splitting (see @sec-gen-dml-plr). Their reasoning is that the procedure inherently (and asymptotically) eliminates the empirical process term of the nuisance estimator's bias, irrespective of whether observations are correlated. Consequently, "bespoke" resampling methods purposing to mitigate training-test set correlation (e.g., cluster-robust or BCR resampling) are to be regarded as unnecessary for cross-fitting.[^146]

[^146]: A brief articulation of their argument may be found in Balkus et al. (2026, pp. 1-3).

Critically appraising their work is outside the scope of this project, and in any case is a task likely to be taken up by the progenitors of cluster-robust and panel-data DML (*inter alia*). Nevertheless, I maintain that BCR-DML remains appropriate, the advent of a debate over cluster-robust cross-fitting's utility notwithstanding. First, Balkus et al. (2026) expressly clarify that their findings pertain to the estimation of $\theta_{0}$, exclusively; indeed, they remind that estimation of $SE$ still requires adjusting for inter-observational correlation, and that model selection (e.g., hyperparameter tuning) may potentially benefit from cross-validation optimizing out-of-sample performance on correlation-aware splits (p. 15). Even on their own terms, then, the cluster-robust paradigm is likely to be broadly useful, irrespective of whether cluster-robust cross-fitting benefits bias reduction theoretically or empirically. Second, although Balkus et al.'s (2026) thesis covers spatial data, it is unclear whether the dependence structure imposed by spatial lagging violates their spatial-dependence assumptions.[^147] Preserving cluster-robust cross-fitting thus seems a safer choice---a view further supported by their simulations, which find that any difference in bias between as-IID and cluster-robust resampling vanishes asymptotically (Balkus et al., 2026, pp. 10-11). Together, these considerations motivate me to not only deploy the BCR-DML method in its entirety, but also import BCR resampling into the tuning phase (as described in @sec-gen-dml-fits-tune).

[^147]: These assumptions specifically extend the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) for dependent data and nuisance-estimator convergence rate to network/spatial data, imposing additional requirements. For more, see Balkus et al. (2026, pp. 11-12).

##### Stacking {#sec-gen-dml-fits-stack}

Ultimately, I carry out the BCR-DML procedure using each of the four "base" or candidate learners introduced in @sec-gen-dml-lrn: lasso, ridge, random forests, and boosted trees. Recall that I presented two general options for proceeding with inference based on these learners' results: selecting the learner with the best out-of-sample performance (e.g., overall or per nuisance part), or aggregating the residuals through an ensemble mechanism such as stacking. Presently, the DML literature does not agree on a preferred learner-selection strategy. Bach et al. (2024b), for example, compare three strategies. The first selects on "combined nuisance loss," an overall-performance metric of the form, in PLR:

$$
RMSE(\hat{m}_{0})*\left(RMSE(\hat{m}_{0}) + RMSE(\hat{\ell}_{0})\right)
$$

The second selects on predictive performance for $Y$, and the third executes stacking. Through their simulations, the authors find that selecting on combined loss yields the lowest predictive error, motivating their endorsement of it; however, they acknowledge that the three methods compare favorably to each other, and stacking is shown to exhibit the smallest dispersion in bias.[^148] By contrast, in their own simulations and applied study, Ahrens et al. (2025b) compare approaches that select the "single-best" performing learner per nuisance part against three different stacking methods. They observe that single-best selection performs similarly to stacking when there indeed exists a clear best learner, but that it otherwise delivers more erratic causal estimates. As such, they advocate for stacking as a safer default.[^149]

[^148]: Predictive error is assessed specifically on mean and median relative RMSE (rRMSE). For a discussion of their exact findings and the formulae for both combined loss and rRMSE, see Bach et al. (2024b, pp. 7, 10-11, & 18).

[^149]: For more on their central findings and recommendations, see Ahrens et al. (2025b, pp. 258 & 265-266).

These perspectives being taken into account, I elect to proceed with stacking---an operation that, in sum, combines the results of base learners through optimized weights, thereby constructing a "super learner" whose predictive performance on the sample is guaranteed to be no worse than that of the best-performing base learner. First, as aforementioned (see @sec-gen-dml-lrn-dcns-regz), the true DGPs for my samples are unknown, rendering the discovery of true best learners unlikely, perhaps even impossible. In this setting, stacking offers a safer path forward; and indeed, even if such a learner were to exist, as Ahrens et al. (2025b) note, stacking would simply approximate single-best selection by assigning said learner a disproportionately-larger weight (p. 258). Second, the formula for combined loss prioritizes performance for the nuisance part estimating the treatment ($\hat{m}_{0}$).[^150] Consequently, those learners better-executing this particular task will tend to be selected under a combined-loss criterion, despite that other learners may perform markedly and systematically better at estimating the outcome ($\hat{\ell}_{0}$). If so, whether combined loss veritably facilitates selection of the overall-best learner would be both theoretically and empirically uncertain. Since my results indeed exhibit such disparities, with tree-based learners generally better at $\hat{\ell}_{0}$ and regularized-regression learners at $\hat{m}_{0}$,[^151] I am further motivated to adopt stacking, a technique endowed with the flexibility to exploit each learner's complementary strengths.

[^150]: To be precise, there are---in effect---two terms that constitute combined loss: the square of $RMSE(\hat{m}_{0})$ (i.e., $MSE(\hat{m}_{0})$) and $RMSE(\hat{\ell}_{0})$ as indexed by $RMSE(\hat{m}_{0})$. $\hat{m}_{0}$ contributes to both of these, and in one is accorded exponential influence. $\hat{\ell}_{0}$, meanwhile, contributes to just one of the terms. Therefore, it is axiomatic that combined loss treats the performance of the treatment estimator, $\hat{m}_{0}$, as as a more important indicator of overall performance.

[^151]: I have saved the MSEs and stacking weights for each learner, results I am happy to provide upon request.

Following Ahrens et al. (2025b), I employ short-stacking as my preferred stacking method. As with many stacking algorithms, short-stacking solves a constrained least squares (CLS) problem that finds a convex combination of non-negative weights summing to one. Specifically, for basic DML:

$$
\begin{align*}
\min_{w_{1}, ..., w_{A}}
\sum_{i = 1}^{n}
\Bigg(
Y_{i} - 
\sum_{a = 1}^{A}
w_{a}
\hat{\ell}_{I_{k(i)}^{c}}^{(a)}
(\mathbf{X}_{i})
\Bigg)^{2}
\\
\text{s.t.}
\;
w_{a}
\geq
0,
\sum_{a = 1}^{A}
|w_{a}|
=
1
\end{align*}
$$

Here, $w_{1}, ..., w_{A}$ are the stacking weights for each $a \in [A] = \{1, ..., A\}$ base learner and $\hat{\ell}_{I_{k(i)}^{c}}^{(a)} (\mathbf{X}_{i})$ the prediction for test-fold observation $i$ using training data $I_{k(i)}^{c}$ (i.e., all folds wherein the $i$th observation is absent). This problem is solved for all nuisance parts, such that in the PLR case, a combination of $A$ weights is found for $\hat{\ell}_{0}$ and $\hat{m}_{0}$ each.[^152] Of course, the short-stacking algorithm is readily adaptable to BCR-DML, since it need only consider predictions for any $(i, j)$ observation made from buffer-aware training data $([N] \backslash I^{b}_{k(i)}) \times ([M] \backslash J_{\ell(j)})$ (see @sec-gen-dml-fits-final-bcr).

[^152]: Note that I have $A$ signify the total number of base learners in lieu of $J$, Ahrens et al.'s (2025b) preferred notation, so as to avoid confusion with my other uses of $J$. For more on the notation and intention of CLS stacking algorithms, including short-stacking, see Ahrens et al. (2025b, pp. 252-254).

Ahrens et al. (2025b) endorse short-stacking over the alternative stacking procedures since it performs competitively at a steep computational discount.[^153] Essentially, short-stacking computes weight combinations directly from the cross-fitted residuals. Heuristically, then, expenses are proportional to $K \times A$ (or $K^{2} \times A$ for two-way cluster-robust DML), the number of cross-fitting folds multiplied by the number of base learners. By contrast, consider conventional and pooled stacking, the chief alternatives to short-stacking. The conventional algorithm cross-validates $V$ times within each cross-fitting training set, generating residuals from which a unique weight combination per $k$th test fold may be derived. Similarly, pooled stacking performs within-training-set cross-validation $V$ times but instead assembles the residuals into a "pooled" dataset, facilitating the computation of a single weight combination. In either case, expenses are heuristically proportional to $K \times V \times A$, which in practice may be far greater than $K \times A$.[^154] Moreover, stacking incorporating a cross-validation layer as such complicates cluster-robust and BCR-DML, since cluster- and buffer-wise disjoint folds must formed $K$ more times (i.e., for each training set). Finally, in their simulation, Ahrens et al. (2025b) find that short-stacking performs similar to or better than conventional and pooled stacking, its structurally-lower costs notwithstanding.[^155] The advantages short-stacking enjoys are thus decisive, furnishing me with ample reason to adopt it.

[^153]: That the number of candidate learners ($A$) should be small vis-à-vis the sample size ($N$) is the only stipulation for this recommendation. Doubtless, it ought to be satisfied in the vast majority of applied settings, including mine (wherein $A = 4$). For more on this condition, see Ahrens et al. (2025b, p. 254).

[^154]: For instance, for two-way cluster-robust DML, if $V = 10$ since $K = 10$, then $V^{2} = 100$, meaning conventional and pooled stacking will basically be $100$-times costlier than short-stacking.

[^155]: For a comprehensive discussion of the alternative stacking algorithms, as well as formulae and visualizations thereof, see Ahrens et al. (2025b, pp. 252-254).

To carry out short-stacking, I borrow source code from [`ddml`](https://thomaswiemann.com/ddml/index.html), a package intended to complement `DoubleML` by enabling short-stacking as proposed by Ahrens et al. (2025b).[^156] In sum, for any sample $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$, I first perform BCR tuning and cross-fitting for all $A$ learners using `DoubleML`. Doing so allows me to construct $\mathbf{\hat{Q}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times R \times p_{1} \times A}$ and $\mathbf{\hat{V}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times R \times p_{1} \times A}$, matrices of cross-fitted residuals for nuisance-part estimates $\hat{\ell}_{0}$ and $\hat{m}_{0}$, respectively.[^157] For $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}$ and $\mathbf{\hat{V}}$ each, I then derive optimal weight sets $\mathbf{W}_{\hat{\ell}_{0}} \in \mathbb{R}^{R \times p_{1} \times A}$ and $\mathbf{W}_{\hat{m}_{0}} \in \mathbb{R}^{R \times p_{1} \times A}$ by solving the `ddml` default CLS algorithm, a non-negative least squares problem summing to one, leveraging the package's source code to do so.[^158] Finally, I solve $\mathbf{W}_{\hat{\ell}_{0}}\mathbf{\hat{Q}}^{T}$ and $\mathbf{W}_{\hat{m}_{0}}\mathbf{\hat{V}}^{T}$, the results of which I sum for every $i$th row, thereby generating matrices of "stacked" residuals $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}_{stack} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times R \times p_{1}}$ and $\mathbf{\hat{V}}_{stack} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times R \times p_{1}}$. These are the basic inputs needed to compute estimated effect(s) $\boldsymbol{\hat{\theta}}_{stack} \in \mathbb{R}^{p_{1}}$ and the accompanying $\mathbf{SE} \in \mathbb{R}^{p_{1}}$, completing the BCR-DML procedure. To perform this final task, I simply borrow the [`DoubleML` source code](https://rdrr.io/cran/DoubleML/src/R/double_ml.R) for cluster-robust DML, deploying $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}_{stack}$, $\mathbf{\hat{V}}_{stack}$, and any other requisite information (e.g., the fold assignments for both observations and clusters).[^159]

[^156]: `DoubleML` offers far more features, such as specifying custom sample splits and conducting cluster-robust inference, and is embedded in the highly-flexible `mlr3` ecosystem, hence why I use it (and its source code) for all DML operations apart from finding the stacking weights. See the [`ddml` webpage](https://thomaswiemann.com/ddml/index.html) for more on this package's general capabilities and purpose as a complement to `DoubleML`.

[^157]: Recall that $R$ denotes the number of cross-fitting rounds and $p_{1}$ the number of treatments. This notation---as well as that for the residuals---first appears in @sec-gen-dml-plr.

[^158]: The default algorithm is denoted by `nnls1`. For the exact source code I implement, see the [`ddml` Github repository](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thomaswiemann/ddml/master/R/ensemble.R).
