[^159]: I have verified that my borrowing of source code replicates whatever would be produced by the packages automatically, and that $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}_{stack}$ and $\mathbf{\hat{V}}_{stack}$ indeed give lower $MSE$s relative to $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}$ and $\mathbf{\hat{V}}$. I am happy to provide the scripts for and results of these "sanity checks" upon request.

Ultimately, having chosen $K^{2}$ cluster-robust DML and $K = 10$, $K^{2} = 100$; and because $R = 3$, there are then $600$ cross-fits for any given $\hat{\theta}_{i,j,l}$: $100$ per nuisance part---namely, $\hat{m}_{0}$ and $\hat{\ell}_{0}$---per $r \in [R]$ round.[^160]

[^160]: As a reminder, I justify my selection of $K$ and $R$ in @sec-gen-dml-plr.

### Pooling {#sec-gen-pool}

The final step of my methodology rounds off the multiple imputation procedure initiated during preprocessing. As discussed in @sec-gen-prep-mi, pooling entails combining the causal statistics found from multiply-imputed datasets $(\mathbf{m}_{i})_{i=1}^{m}$ and performing inference therefrom. Following the procedure set forth in Rubin (1987, pp. 76-77), the `mice` package pools by:[^161]

[^161]: The following summary adapts those found in [Heymans & Eekhout (2019)](https://bookdown.org/mwheymans/bookmi/rubins-rules.html#significance-testing) and [Van Buren (2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-whyandwhen.html).

1.  Taking the mean of estimated effects $(\hat{\theta}_{i})_{i = 1}^{m}$. Namely:

$$\begin{align*}
\bar{\theta}
=
\frac{1}{m}
\sum_{i = 1}^{m}
\hat{\theta}_{i}
\end{align*}$$

2.  Letting $(U_{i})_{i = 1}^{m} = (SE_{i}^{2})_{i = 1}^{m}$, finding the within-imputation variance:

$$\begin{align*}
\bar{U}
=
\frac{1}{m}
\sum_{i = 1}^{m}
U_{i}
\end{align*}$$

3.  Finding the between-imputation variance:

$$\begin{align*}
B
=
\frac{1}{m - 1}
\sum_{i = 1}^{m}
(\hat{\theta}_{i} - \bar{\theta})^{2}
\end{align*}$$

4.  Computing the total variance:

$$\begin{align*}
T
=
\bar{U}
+
(1 + \frac{1}{m})
B
\end{align*}$$

5.  With pooled estimate $\bar{\theta}$ and standard error $\sqrt{T}$---and for the null hypothesis $H_{0}: \theta = 0$---computing the $t$-statistic:[^162]

[^162]: The formula below assumes the use of a two-tailed test, in which case the sign of the $t$-statistic is irrelevant. In [Van Buuren (2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-inference.html), the formula is given by: $t = \frac{\theta - \bar{\theta}}{\sqrt{T}}$.

$$\begin{align*}
t = \frac{\bar{\theta}}{\sqrt{T}}
\end{align*}$$

6.  With $df$ degrees of freedom, constructing a confidence interval:

$$\begin{align*}
\bar{\theta}
\pm
t_{1-\alpha/2, df}
\sqrt{T}
\end{align*}$$

In modern implementations, $df$ is found as per the "Barnard-Rubin adjustment":

$$\begin{align*}
df
=
\frac{df_{old} * df_{obs}}{df_{old} + df_{obs}}
\end{align*}$$

Here, $df_{old}$ refers to Rubin's original degrees-of-freedom formula and $df_{obs}$ to the estimated observed-data degrees of freedom. Specifically, where $\lambda = \frac{B + B/m}{T}$ and $df_{com}$ is the difference between the $n$ sample size and $k$ number of parameters (i.e., $df_{com} = n - k$):[^163]

[^163]: [Van Buuren (2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-whyandwhen.html#sec:varianceratios) remarks that $\lambda$ "can be interpreted as the proportion of the variation attributable to the missing data."

$$\begin{align*}
df_{old}
=
\frac{m - 1}{\lambda^{2}}
\\
df_{obs}
=
\frac{df_{com} + 1}{df_{com} + 3}
df_{com}
(1 - \lambda)
\end{align*}$$

However, because I set $df_{com} = \infty$ (see @sec-gen-prep-tl), my formula for $df$ simply reduces to that of $df_{old}$.[^164]

[^164]: For more on the implication of setting $df_{com} = \infty$, see [Van Buuren (2018)](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-whyandwhen.html#eq:oldnu).

So it is that the results from all $(m_{i})_{i=1}^{5}$ iterations of datasets $\mathbf{v}_{i,j,l}$ are consolidated, delivering final causal estimates $\hat{\theta}_{j,l}$ (i.e., $\bar{\theta}_{j,l}$) and their attendant inferential data. These form the basis of my conclusions, the beginnings of which I proffer in @sec-res.

![Pooling Flowchart. Note that $\hat{\theta}_{j,l}$ is the mean of all $\hat{\theta}_{i,j,l}$.](/Users/briankey/Documents/Academics/Northwestern/dissertation/visualizations/drafts/pool_flow_viz.png){#fig-pool-flow}

### Replication {#sec-gen-rep}

In each chapter, I also run models that approximate those of the literature inspiring my work, the main points of departure (where appropriate) being (1.) the substitution of HR Scores for the authors' outcomes and my selected treatments for theirs, and (2.) the use of both unimputed (in line with the authors' methodologies) and multiply-imputed data. I do so to test whether the introduction of new key variables and/or multiple imputation immediately yields divergent results. More on these replications can be found in @sec-res-ch1-rep, @sec-res-ch2-rep, and @sec-res-ch3-rep.

## Results {#sec-res}

### General Remarks {#sec-res-gen-rem}

In the interest of efficiency, I now preface my results by elaborating on the final design choices common to multiple chapters. These follow mainly from theoretical considerations, encompassing (1.) covariate selection, (2.) fixed effects, (3.) regional model variants, and (4.) interaction-term treatments.

#### Covariates {#sec-res-gen-rem-covar}

In @sec-gen-prep-dw-covar, I enumerated the covariates featured in all three chapters. My rationale for their inclusion may be summarized as follows:

1.  Accession to PTAs/BITs and exposure to economic sanctions may correlate with quality of democratic institutions. Hypotheses for these possible relationships include:

    i.  Democracies, being intrinsically more prone to complying with human-rights standards and the accords enshrining them, may have fewer qualms about agreeing to hard PTAs in the first place (Spilker & Böhmelt, 2013, p. 352).
    ii. States with poor democratic institutions may be motivated to improve their credibility among foreign investors and thus seek membership in more BITs.[^165]
    iii. States with poor (or decaying) democratic institutions are naturally more vulnerable to becoming targets of those sanctions expressly intended to improve democracy and human-rights respect (Peez, 2025, p. 16).

    The democracy scores I employ are ultimately meant to control for these scenarios. To avoid privileging a single conceptualization or measure of democracy, a typical practice in the underlying literature,[^166] I select all 26 of V-Dem's high- and mid-level indices. Importantly, I ignore the far-more numerous lower-level V-Dem indicators to contain computational expenses, and since many of these are aggregated into (and thus captured by) the mid- and high-level indices in any case.

2.  In a similar vein, I also include Polity and Regime Durability. Polity serves as the proxy for democracy in the PTAs/BITs literature, so its inclusion helps clarify comparability with the works thereof. Regime Durability---the number of years since the last major, structural change in a state's regime[^167]---performs a similar function, since it figures in these pieces as well. However, it may also be seen as capturing the recency of "trigger events,"[^168] which precipitate meaningful changes to institutional quality and hence susceptibility to PTA/BIT accession or economic sanctions. For example, young democracies may consent to harder PTAs to "signal their commitment" to more robust human-rights standards (Spilker & Böhmelt, 2013, p. 352). Alternatively, the proximate causes of economic sanctions may lie in sudden, unignorable instances of repression or backsliding.

3.  The PTAs/BITs literature conditions on a set of World Development Indicators (WDIs) that generally includes:

    i.  Trade openness---i.e., the sum of exports and imports of goods and services as a percentage of GDP. The literature adduces research finding that flows of international commerce may influence human-rights respect, for better or worse.[^169] Although correlations with the treatment(s) are not explicitly theorized, one may plausibly expect trade-favoring states to exhibit commensurate sympathy to liberal economic treaties, including PTAs and BITs.
    ii. Foreign direct investment (FDI). Hafner-Burton's (2005) measure sums the absolute values of net FDI inflows and outflows (p. 617), whereas Bodea & Ye (2020) focus on the inflows component (p. 965).[^170] In either case, the foregoing hypothesis linking international economic transactions and human-rights respect motivates their inclusion. However, it is likewise natural to intuit that openness to FDI correlates with agreeability to treaties such as PTAs and BITs.
    iii. Population density (per square kilometer). Explaining its inclusion, Hafner-Burton (2005, p. 617) and Spilker & Böhment (2013, p. 351) point to scholarship raising concerns about population pressure driving resource scarcity and hence higher rates of repression. If population density affects human-rights respect in this way, however, then it would be logical to anticipate a similar link to democracy, a possible determinant of PTA/BIT membership (for reasons aforementioned).

    Peez (2025) does not use any of these covariates. Yet it seems plausible that sanctions senders might be warier of targeting countries better-integrated into the global economy, lest doing so disrupt (directly or indirectly) critical transactional flows, harming their own economies in the process. Conversely, economically-isolated (or "-weak") states---mattering less to the economies of sender states---may be more vulnerable to sanctions. Targets' economic importance, captured by signals such as trade openness and FDI inflows/outflows, may thus be fairly suspected as a confounding factor. Moreover, any relationship between population density and democracy would naturally have implications for economic-sanctions vulnerability.

    The group of WDIs initially used in the PTAs/BITs literature therefore seems appropriate for the entire dissertation. For the most part, I utilize consistent, untransformed versions of the WDIs, the only exception being the FDI metrics. Specifically, in Chapter 1, I recreate the single measure of FDI in Hafner-Burton (2005), thus ensuring direct comparability thereto. In Chapter 2, on the other hand, I generally follow Bodea & Ye's (2020) approach, including both the inflows and outflows components as separate regressors under the assumption that the latter may also influence amenability to BITs.[^171] This design choice is repeated for Chapter 3, since I prefer the safety of variables in their original form wherever possible.

4.  Gross domestic product per capita (GDPpc)---a proxy for national wealth---is put to work throughout the underlying literature. In the PTAs/BITs articles, GDPpc controls for the link between poverty and repression (Hafner-Burton, 2005, p. 617; Spilker & Böhmelt, p. 352); however, it is also reasonable to postulate a connection between wealth and PTA/BIT membership. Specifically, rich states may look to PTAs/BITs as a means of guaranteeing or locking in favorable market conditions, whereas poorer states may do so aiming for improved market access and accelerated development. Peez (2025), by contrast, rationalizes the use of GDPpc on a potential link to treatment assignment, theorizing that economically "weak" states may be more vulnerable to becoming sanctions targets (p. 14). Regardless, the possible confoundedness (explicitly or implicitly) motivating GDPpc's use as a common covariate seems sufficiently credible to warrant its continued inclusion in my own models.

    The relevant literature do not deploy gross domestic product (GDP) or population as controls. However, an effect on treatment assignment by present or future market size---for which GDP and population serve as proxies---needs little to entertain. First, the same dynamics pushing wealthy or poor states to join PTAs/BITs may well apply, respectively, to large or small states, who may seek out such treaties to lock in economic predominance or jumpstart growth. Also, large-market states may enjoy greater insulation from sanctions than small-market states, whose current or projected contributions to the global economy may be registered as less significant in the cost-benefit analyses of sanctions senders. Therefore, there exists adequate reason to incorporate GDP and population as controls throughout, too.[^172]

    The exact variables I choose are Fariss et al.'s (2022). Generated from a latent-variable model drawing on myriad measurements of GDP, GDPpc, and population, their own estimates are designed to provide enhanced measurement coverage, certainty, and resistance to bias than any of their model's individual inputs.[^173] As such, these measures are likely safer than those that do not (e.g., the WDIs for GDP, GDPpc, and population, which also form a share of the foregoing inputs), making them worthy for inclusion in models such as mine.

5.  The final batch of predictors I invariably implement endeavors to account for impacts occasioned by the threat or onset of financial crises. A diversity of observers---including international organizations (e.g., the United Nations), watchdogs (e.g., Amnesty International), and more---have cast financial crises as a major catalyst of repression (Mukherjee & Yadav, 2024, pp. 16-17). The story typically told for this causal link is straightforward: financial crises, whose ramifications are wide-ranging and devastating, compel many disaffected citizens to mobilize against their governments, who in turn greet their dissent with repression.[^174] Mukherjee & Yadav (2024) complicate this image by pointing out that while it does not "inevitably" follow, as traditional accounts would have it (p. 17), repression is indeed a possible outcome of financial crises, particularly amid a "twin" currency and sudden-stop crisis and International Monetary Fund (IMF) program participation.[^175] In any case, the literature agrees that a correlation between financial crises and repression is to be expected in at least some cases, raising the possibility of its role as a confounder in my modeling.

    Currency crises and sudden stops---the foci of Mukherjee & Yadav's (2024) study---are especially important to consider. The proximate cause of the former are usually speculative attacks by foreign-exchange traders. Though the conditions undergirding and triggers of these attacks have been elaborated by multiple "generations" of research, their upshot is the same: depletion of foreign-currency reserves (e.g., U.S. dollars) and galloping domestic-currency depreciation.[^176] Similarly, though ascribed to a variety of sources in the literature, sudden-stop crises all share the same basic pattern: a dramatic retraction of capital inflows (e.g., foreign-portfolio investment), undercutting national outputs and foreign-currency reserves in turn. In this way, sudden stops may effectuate or contribute to currency crises themselves.[^177] To avert, ameliorate, or resolve these crises, states may look to policies that improve their balance of payments (BoP) and thus rebuild their foreign-currency reserves.[^178] Of these, perhaps the most well-known is assistance from the IMF, the international "lender of last resort" (Mukherjee & Yadav, 2024, pp. 76-77). Yet it is rational to expect states to seek relief in other sources, too, including liberal trade and investment treaties. Indeed, acceding to these would in theory mitigate salient short- and long-term contributors to the financial crises at issue. In the short-term, they would lower the costs facing prospective investors and importers from foreign states, unlocking the kinds of transcations conducive to replenishing reserve currencies. Additionally, they would signal commitment to macroeconomic stability, encouraging such transactions still further. In the long-term, these benefits would compound, fueling a virtuous cycle marginalizing the specter of financial-crisis outbreak. That states follow this logic is even supported anecdotally: negotiations for a [free trade agreement between Sri Lanka and Thailand](https://investmentpolicy.unctad.org/international-investment-agreements/treaties/bit/5136/sri-lanka---thailand-fta-2024-) were accelerated in 2023, and concluded the following year, expressly to help the former rebuild its foreign-currency reserves amid its own financial crisis.[^179] Therefore, the clear implication is that currency and sudden-stop crises might well be confounders in chapters 1 and 2, increasing not only the likelihood of repression, but also PTAs/BITs accession. Although these crises may not directly trigger sanctions, their deleterious impact on democratic institutions may heighten vulnerability thereto, rendering financial crises a possible confounder in Chapter 3 as well.[^180]

    Controlling for currency and sudden-stop crises is mostly simple to achieve by dint of publicly-available sources. Specifically, although Mukherjee & Yadav's (2024) replication data are as yet unpublished, to the best of my knowledge, versions of the variables cited as informing their own are easy to locate. First, Nguyen et al. (2022) provide an updated version of the Laeven & Valencia (2020) Systemic Banking Crises Database, a comprehensive tracker of several financial-crisis types, including currency crises.[^181] Most helpfully, Nguyen et al.'s (2022) dataset is rendered in country-year panel format, thereby offering a currency-crisis indicator ready for use in models such as mine. Unfortunately, none of these datasets contain an indicator for sudden-stop crises, specifically, and the sources Mukherjee & Yadav (2024, p. 152) adduce for constructing theirs exhibit poor coverage.[^182] However, because sudden stops become currency crises when sufficiently severe (Nguyen et al., 2022, p. 3), sudden-stop crises frequenly coincide with currency crises; and indeed, in Mukherjee & Yadav's (2024) sample of developing countries, the two co-occured approximately two-thirds of the time (p. 14). Consequently, following Nguyen et al. (2022), who aver that a sudden-stop crisis "can be identified through a currency crisis" (p. 3), I proceed with their currency-crisis indicator alone, presupposing that it suffices to capture sudden-stop crises as well.

    To model the possible link between IMF program participation and financial-crisis onset---and, ergo, PTAs/BITs accession or financial-sanctions imposition---I also incorporate a 2023 update to Vreeland's (2007) indicator, which simply registers whether a country was party to any IMF arrangement during a given year.[^183] Though applying a somewhat-different taxonomy of eligible arrangements to form their own indicator, Mukherjee & Yadav (2024) cite his original dataset as a source (pp. 154-155), making Vreeland's indicator a credible alternative thereto. Finally, it is possible that states seek to adopt some liberal economic policies---including PTAs/BITs and those attending IMF programs---to improve their BoP in preemption of a full-bore crisis. Therefore, to capture the relative "health" of a state's BoP, which may figure prominently in their projections and calculi, I include BoP as a percentage of GDP. To create this variable, I simply take the BoP figures provided by the IMF and divide them by an unscaled version of Fariss et al.'s (2022) GDP estimates.[^184]

[^165]: Bodea & Ye (2020) describe this theory but conclude that the evidence supporting it is "weak" (p. 957). Still, including democracy scores is sensible lest their view be incorrect.

## Conclusion {#sec-cncl}

### Appendix E: PLR Score Function to OLS {#sec-appx-e}

Recall from @sec-gen-dml-plr that the generic DML estimator solves the moment condition:

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I}\psi(\mathbf{S};\hat{\theta}_{0},\hat{\eta}_{0}) = 0
\end{align*}$$

Also recall the standard PLR score function, which may be further expanded:

$$\begin{align*}
\psi(\mathbf{S};\theta,\eta) := [\mathbf{Y} - \ell(\mathbf{X}) - \theta(\mathbf{D} - m(\mathbf{X}))][\mathbf{D} - m(\mathbf{X})]\ \\
= -\theta(\mathbf{D} - m(\mathbf{X}))^{2} + (\mathbf{Y} - \ell(\mathbf{X}))(\mathbf{D} - m(\mathbf{X}))
\end{align*}$$

Solving the moment-condition estimator gives:[^185]

[^185]: The distribution of the mean operator $\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I}\right)$ and the constant ($-\hat{\theta}$) follows from the linearity of expectation.

$$\begin{align*}
0 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I}[-\hat{\theta}_{0}(\mathbf{D} - \hat{m}(\mathbf{X}))^{2} + (\mathbf{Y} - \hat{\ell}(\mathbf{X}))(\mathbf{D} - \hat{m}(\mathbf{X}))] \\
\Longrightarrow 0 = -\hat{\theta}_{0}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I}(\mathbf{D} - \hat{m}(\mathbf{X}))^{2} + \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I}(\mathbf{Y} - \hat{\ell}(\mathbf{X}))(\mathbf{D} - \hat{m}(\mathbf{X})) \\
\Longrightarrow \hat{\theta}_{0}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I}(\mathbf{D} - \hat{m}(\mathbf{X}))^{2} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I}(\mathbf{Y} - \hat{\ell}(\mathbf{X}))(\mathbf{D} - \hat{m}(\mathbf{X})) \\
\Longrightarrow \hat{\theta}_{0} = \frac{\sum_{i \in I}(\mathbf{Y} - \hat{\ell}(\mathbf{X}))(\mathbf{D} - \hat{m}(\mathbf{X}))}{\sum_{i \in I} (\mathbf{D} - \hat{m}(\mathbf{X}))^{2}}
\end{align*}$$

Where:

$$\begin{align*}
\mathbf{\hat{Q}} = \mathbf{Y} - \hat{\ell}_{0}(\mathbf{X}) \\
\mathbf{\hat{V}} = \mathbf{D} - \hat{m}_{0}(\mathbf{X})
\end{align*}$$

And where $\hat{\ell}_{0}$ and $\hat{m}_{0}$ are plug-in estimators of the conditional expectations:

$$\begin{align*}
\ell_{0}(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}|\mathbf{X}] \\
m_{0}(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}|\mathbf{X}]
\end{align*}$$

Now, consider a simple linear regression, wherein OLS predicts an outcome $\mathbf{Y}$ from a single treatment $\mathbf{D}$.[^186] The true coefficient on the explanator may be expressed as:[^187]

[^186]: To wit: $\mathbf{Y} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\mathbf{D} + \epsilon_{i}$

[^187]: That is, $\beta_{1} = \frac{\text{Cov}(\mathbf{D}, \mathbf{Y})}{\text{Var}(\mathbf{D})}$. In the bivariate case, $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}] = \bar{\mathbf{D}}$ and $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}] = \bar{\mathbf{Y}}$. The basic formula may be found in Rice (2007, p. 544), for example, albeit in scalar notation.

$$\begin{align*}
\beta_{1} = \frac{\sum_{i \in I}(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y}])(\mathbf{D} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}])}{\sum_{i \in I} (\mathbf{D} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}])^{2}}
\end{align*}$$

Or, in the multivariate case, with covariates $\mathbf{X}$, regressing residualized $\mathbf{Y}$ on residualized $\mathbf{D}$ implies (as per the FWL Theorem):

$$\begin{align*}
\beta_{1} = \frac{\sum_{i \in I}(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Y|X}])(\mathbf{D} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D|X}])}{\sum_{i \in I} (\mathbf{D} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D|X}])^{2}} \\
= \frac{\sum_{i \in I}(\mathbf{Y} - \ell_{0}(\mathbf{X}))(\mathbf{D} - m_{0}(\mathbf{X}))}{\sum_{i \in I} (\mathbf{D} - m_{0}(\mathbf{X}))^{2}}
\end{align*}$$

The solutions to $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ and the sample analogue $\hat{\beta}_{1}$ of $\beta_{1}$ are thus the selfsame, sufficing to illustrate how partialling out---that is, regressing $\mathbf{\hat{Q}}$ on $\mathbf{\hat{V}}$ to obtain $\hat{\theta}_{0}$ using OLS---implies the standard PLR score function.

### Appendix F: Example of Cluster-Robust DML Resampling {#sec-appx-f}

To better-illustrate the resampling procedure introduced in @sec-gen-dml-fits-final, consider a basic panel dataset comprised of countries $c \in [C] = \{1, ..., C\}$ and years $t \in [T] = \{1, ..., T\}$.[^188] In addition, let $C = 4$, $T = 4$, and $K = 2$. Now, suppose that the $C$ countries and $T$ years are randomly partitioned into the following initial subgroups:

[^188]: Recalling the notation used in @sec-gen-dml-fits-final, $C$ equates to $N$ and $T$ to $M$.

$$\begin{align*}
I_{1} = \{c_{1}, c_{3}\} \qquad J_{1} = \{t_{2}, t_{3}\} \\
I_{2} = \{c_{2}, c_{4}\} \qquad J_{2} = \{t_{1}, t_{4}\}
\end{align*}$$

Per the two-way splitting operation, these form $K^{2} = 4$ folds:

$$\begin{align*}
I_{1} \times J_{1} = \{(c_{1},t_{2}), (c_{1},t_{3}), (c_{3},t_{2}), (c_{3},t_{3})\} \\
I_{1} \times J_{2} = \{(c_{1},t_{1}), (c_{1},t_{4}), (c_{3},t_{1}), (c_{3},t_{4}\}) \\
I_{2} \times J_{1} = \{(c_{2},t_{2}), (c_{2},t_{3}), (c_{4},t_{2}), (c_{4},t_{3})\} \\
I_{2} \times J_{2} = \{(c_{2},t_{1}), (c_{2},t_{4}), (c_{4},t_{1}), (c_{4},t_{4})\}
\end{align*}$$

Each is treated once as a test set, evaluating fits from corresponding training sets:

$$\begin{align*}
I_{1}^{c} \times J_{1}^{c} = I_{2} \times J_{2} \\
I_{1}^{c} \times J_{2}^{c} = I_{2} \times J_{1} \\
I_{2}^{c} \times J_{1}^{c} = I_{1} \times J_{2} \\
I_{2}^{c} \times J_{2}^{c} = I_{1} \times J_{1}
\end{align*}$$

How cluster-robust cross-fitting compares to the conventional approach summarized in @sec-gen-dml-plr is therefore clear. On the one hand, both guarantee observation-wise mutual exclusivity, guarding against the severest type of data leakage: observations appearing on both sides of the same training-test set pair. On the other, cluster-robust cross-fitting goes a step further, enforcing group-wise independence as well. This is achieved by forming training sets from only those observations disjoint from the test set on all specified dimensions (e.g., country and year). Consequently, in the multiway case, these training sets are invariably smaller than those that would be formed under conventional sample splitting, whereby all observations not belonging to the test set simply constitute the training set.
